notes.front: What is a cash account?
notes.back: A brokerage account in which the investor must pay the full amount for securities bought, without borrowing from the broker-dealer.
notes.explanation: Borrowing to pay for trades is trading on margin, which the glossary says a cash account does not allow.
notes.example: Like paying for shopping with a debit card: the money must already be there.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Cash Account”, “Cash Account”
notes.evidence: A cash account is a type of brokerage account in which the investor must pay the full amount for securities purchased. An investor using a cash account is not allowed to borrow funds from his or her broker-dealer in order to pay for transactions in the account ( trading on margin )

notes.front: What is a margin account?
notes.back: A brokerage account in which the broker-dealer lends the investor cash to buy securities, using the account as collateral.
notes.explanation: The glossary adds that margin increases purchasing power but also exposes investors to the potential for larger losses.
notes.example: Like a loan secured on the goods you buy with it, but the goods are shares.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Margin Account”, “Margin Account”
notes.evidence: A “margin account” is a type of brokerage account in which the broker-dealer lends the investor cash, using the account as collateral, to purchase securities. Margin increases investors’ purchasing power, but also exposes investors to the potential for larger losses.

notes.front: What is Regulation T (Reg T)?
notes.back: The Federal Reserve Board’s regulation of credit by brokers and dealers, whose rules govern cash accounts and margin accounts alike.
notes.explanation: The bulletin ties Reg T’s credit rules to buying in a cash account; the same regulation also sets margin-account rules, such as the 50 percent initial margin.
notes.example: Like a central bank setting the deposit you must put down on a loan, but for buying shares.
notes.source: SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy, Updated Investor Bulletin: Trading in Cash Accounts, “Cash accounts and Regulation T”
notes.evidence: The credit extension provisions of the Federal Reserve Board’s Regulation T govern an investor’s use of a cash account to purchase securities.

notes.front: What is a margin call?
notes.back: A demand that a margin investor provide the broker with additional cash or securities because the securities’ price has fallen.
notes.explanation: The call can come from time to time, whenever the stock’s price falls after the initial margin payment.
notes.example: Like a lender asking for a bigger deposit when the house it lent against loses value.
notes.source: SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy, Investor Bulletin: Understanding Margin Accounts, “Margin calls”
notes.evidence: Investors who put up an initial margin payment for a stock may, from time to time, be required to provide the broker with additional cash or securities if the price of the stock falls (a “margin call”).

notes.front: What is maintenance margin (the maintenance requirement)?
notes.back: The minimum equity a customer must keep in a margin account at all times after buying: securities’ value minus the amount owed to the firm.
notes.explanation: Equity here means the value of the securities less what the customer owes the firm.
notes.example: Like a minimum balance on a bank account, but measured as your share of the value of shares bought partly with borrowed money.
notes.source: SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy, Investor Bulletin: Understanding Margin Accounts, “Maintenance requirements”
notes.evidence: This “maintenance requirement” specifies the minimum amount of equity you must maintain in your margin account at all times. The equity in your margin account is the value of your securities less how much you owe to your brokerage firm.

notes.front: What is a discretionary account?
notes.back: An account in which the customer has given a broker authority to make investment decisions for them, which needs written legal authorisation.
notes.explanation: The bulletin says investors generally make their own decisions, and that such authority may be temporary or limited.
notes.example: Like giving a friend your house keys with permission to redecorate, but for trading your account.
notes.source: SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy, Investor Bulletin: How to Open a Brokerage Account, “Discretionary authority”
notes.evidence: In a brokerage account, you will generally make your own investment decisions. In some situations, you may grant temporary or limited "discretionary authority" to a broker to make decisions for you on your account. If you want someone else to have discretionary trading authority on your account, you will need to provide him or her with written legal authorization.

notes.front: What is a wrap account?
notes.back: An investment account in which one “wrapped” fee, or fees, covers all management, brokerage and administrative expenses.
notes.explanation: The glossary says the fee is generally based on the account’s total market value.
notes.example: Like an all-inclusive holiday: one price covers the room, meals and trips.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Wrap Account”, “Wrap Account”
notes.evidence: A wrap account is an investment account where a "wrapped" fee or fees cover all of the management, brokerage and administrative expenses for the account. The fee or fees are generally based on the total market value of the investment account.

notes.front: What is an individual account?
notes.back: An account owned by one person; for bank deposits, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation calls this a single account.
notes.explanation: The brochure’s definition turns on two points: one owner, and no named beneficiaries.
notes.example: Like a library card in one name only, but for investments.
notes.source: FDIC, Your Insured Deposits, “Single Accounts”
notes.evidence: A Single Account is a deposit owned by one person with no beneficiaries.

notes.front: What is joint tenants with right of survivorship (JTWROS)?
notes.back: Joint ownership by two or more people under which, when one owner dies, the surviving owner holds the property.
notes.explanation: Publication 559’s example of joint tenants with right of survivorship has the survivor acquire the dead owner’s interest and add its value to the survivor’s basis.
notes.example: Like two people sharing a car so that, if one dies, the other simply keeps driving it.
notes.source: IRS Publication 559, Survivors, Executors, and Administrators, ““Joint interest””, p. 20
notes.evidence: Figure the surviving tenant's new basis of jointly owned property (joint tenancy or tenancy by the entirety) by adding the surviving tenant's original basis in the property to the value of the part of the property included in the decedent's estate
introduces: joint tenants with right of survivorship
uses: joint tenants with right of survivorship

notes.front: What is a tenants in common account?
notes.back: A joint account owned by two or more people as tenants in common, one of the forms of joint ownership state law allows.
notes.explanation: The brochure lists it beside joint tenants with right of survivorship and tenants by the entirety as ways to own a joint account.
notes.example: Like two friends co-owning a flat in stated shares, but for an account.
notes.source: FDIC, Your Insured Deposits, “Joint Accounts”
notes.evidence: FDIC insurance covers joint accounts owned in any manner conforming to applicable state law, such as joint tenants with right of survivorship, tenants by the entirety, and tenants in common.
uses: joint tenants with right of survivorship

notes.front: What is a corporate account, and how can a firm verify the customer exists?
notes.back: An account opened for a corporation; documents such as certified articles of incorporation or a government-issued business licence show the entity exists.
notes.explanation: The customer identification rule names these documents for a customer that is not an individual.
notes.example: Like a company opening a bank account: the bank asks for the company’s founding papers, not a passport.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.220 (Customer identification programs for broker-dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.220(a)(2)(ii)(A)”
notes.evidence: For a person other than an individual (such as a corporation, partnership or trust), documents showing the existence of the entity, such as certified articles of incorporation, a government-issued business license, a partnership agreement, or a trust instrument.

notes.front: What is a (formal) revocable trust?
notes.back: A written trust, often called a living or family trust, whose owner controls the trust assets during his or her lifetime.
notes.explanation: The brochure says such trusts are written and created for estate planning purposes.
notes.example: Like a will you can rewrite at any time, except the assets are already held in the trust.
notes.source: FDIC, Your Insured Deposits, “Trust Accounts”
notes.evidence: Formal Revocable Trusts - known as living or family trusts – are written trusts created for estate planning purposes. The owner controls the deposits and other assets in the trust during his or her lifetime.

notes.front: What is an irrevocable trust?
notes.back: A trust into which the owner contributes property and gives up all power to cancel or change the trust.
notes.explanation: The brochure says it is set up by statute or a written trust agreement.
notes.example: Like posting a gift you can no longer take back.
notes.source: FDIC, Your Insured Deposits, “Trust Accounts”
notes.evidence: Irrevocable Trusts are deposit accounts held in connection with a trust established by statute or a written trust agreement in which the owner contributes deposits or other property to the trust and gives up all power to cancel or change the trust.

notes.front: What is the Uniform Transfers to Minors Act (UTMA)?
notes.back: A law under which any kind of property can be transferred to a custodian for the benefit of a minor.
notes.explanation: The manual contrasts it with the older Uniform Gifts to Minors Act, which permitted only gifts of cash or securities.
notes.example: Like an aunt handing shares to a trusted adult to look after for her nephew until he comes of age.
notes.source: Social Security POMS SI 01120.205, Uniform Transfers to Minors Act, “Background”
notes.evidence: Under the UTMA, any kind of property, real or personal, tangible or intangible, can be transferred to a custodian for the benefit of a minor. Under UGMA, only gifts of cash or securities are permitted.

notes.front: What is a partnership account, and what address does the firm record for it?
notes.back: An account opened for a partnership; as a customer that is not an individual, its address is a principal place of business.
notes.explanation: The customer identification rule gives corporations, partnerships and trusts a principal place of business in place of a home address.
notes.example: Like a firm of three accountants opening one account in the firm’s name at its office address.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.220 (Customer identification programs for broker-dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.220(a)(2)(i)(A)”

notes.front: What is an individual retirement account (IRA)?
notes.back: An account giving tax advantages for retirement saving, to which you can contribute each year up to the maximum the tax authority allows.
notes.explanation: The glossary lists several types, including traditional and Roth IRAs.
notes.example: Like a savings jar the tax authority treats kindly, as long as it is kept for retirement.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Individual Retirement Account (IRA)”, “Individual Retirement Account (IRA)”
notes.evidence: Individual Retirement Accounts (IRAs) provide tax advantages for retirement savings. You can contribute each year up to the maximum amount allowed by the Internal Revenue Service. There are several types of IRAs available - traditional IRAs, Roth IRAs, SEP IRAs, and SIMPLE IRAs.

notes.front: What is a Roth IRA?
notes.back: An IRA, designated as Roth when set up, whose contributions cannot be deducted but whose qualified distributions are tax-free.
notes.explanation: So the tax benefit comes at withdrawal rather than at contribution.
notes.example: Like paying tax on the seeds so the harvest is tax-free.
notes.source: IRS, Roth IRAs, “Roth IRAs”
notes.evidence: You cannot deduct contributions to a Roth IRA. - If you satisfy the requirements, qualified distributions are tax-free.

notes.front: What is a qualified plan?
notes.back: An employer’s stock bonus, pension or profit-sharing plan for the exclusive benefit of employees or their beneficiaries that meets tax-code requirements.
notes.explanation: Publication 575 says meeting those requirements earns special tax benefits, such as tax deferral for employer contributions.
notes.example: Like a company pension scheme that has passed the tax authority’s inspection.
notes.source: IRS Publication 575, Pension and Annuity Income, ““Qualified employee plan””, p. 4
notes.evidence: A qualified employee plan is an employer’s stock bonus, pension, or profit-sharing plan that is for the exclusive benefit of employees or their beneficiaries and that meets Internal Revenue Code requirements. It qualifies for special tax benefits, such as tax deferral for employer contributions

notes.front: What is a 401(k) plan?
notes.back: An employer-sponsored retirement savings plan giving employees a choice of investment options, typically mutual funds.
notes.explanation: In a traditional 401(k), part of pre-tax salary is invested in the options each employee chooses.
notes.example: Like a workplace savings pot fed straight from your payslip before tax.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “401(k) Plan”, “401(k) Plan”
notes.evidence: An employer-sponsored retirement savings plan that gives employees a choice of investment options, typically mutual funds. Employees who participate in a traditional 401(k) plan have a portion of their pre-tax salary invested directly in the option or options they choose.

notes.front: What is a 403(b) plan?
notes.back: A tax-deferred retirement savings programme for employees of public schools, certain non-profits and some members of the clergy.
notes.explanation: The glossary describes it as tax-deferred and limits it to those three groups of employees.
notes.example: Like a 401(k), but for a state-school teacher or a charity worker.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “403(b) Plan”, “403(B) Plan”
notes.evidence: A type of tax-deferred retirement savings program available to employees of public schools, certain non-profits, and some members of the clergy.

notes.front: What is a defined benefit plan?
notes.back: A pension plan whose employer sponsor promises the plan’s investments will provide a specified monthly benefit at retirement.
notes.explanation: Because the benefit is promised, the glossary says the employer bears the investment risks.
notes.example: Like a guaranteed monthly pension cheque whatever the markets do.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Defined Benefit Plan”, “Defined Benefit Plan”
notes.evidence: Defined benefit plans also are known as pension plans. Employers sponsor defined benefit plans and promise the plan's investments will provide you with a specified monthly benefit at retirement. The employer bears the investment risks.

notes.front: What is a defined contribution plan?
notes.back: A retirement plan, such as a 401(k), that promises no specific payment; the employee, employer or both pay into the employee’s own account.
notes.explanation: With no promised payment, the glossary says the employee bears the investment risks.
notes.example: Like a savings pot whose final size depends on what went in and how it grew.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Defined Contribution Plan”, “Defined Contribution Plan”
notes.evidence: A retirement savings plan, such as a 401(k) plan, that does not promise a specific payment upon retirement. In these plans, the employee or the employer (or both) contribute to the employee's individual account. The employee bears the investment risks.

notes.front: What is a required minimum distribution (RMD)?
notes.back: The minimum amount an IRA owner or plan participant must withdraw each year, starting with the year they reach age 73.
notes.explanation: The tax authority lets the first one be delayed to 1 April of the following year.
notes.example: Like a rule that you must start eating from a stored harvest once you reach a certain age.
notes.source: IRS, Retirement plan and IRA required minimum distributions FAQs, “Q3”
notes.evidence: You must take your first required minimum distribution for the year in which you reach age 73. However, you can delay taking the first RMD until April 1 of the following year.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: What is money laundering?
notes.back: The process of making illegally gained proceeds (“dirty money”) appear legal (“clean”).
notes.explanation: FinCEN says it typically involves three steps: placement, layering and integration.
notes.example: Like washing a stolen car’s paperwork so it can be sold openly.
notes.source: FinCEN, History of Anti-Money Laundering Laws, “History of Anti-Money Laundering Laws”
notes.evidence: Money laundering is the process of making illegally-gained proceeds (i.e. "dirty money") appear legal (i.e. "clean"). Typically, it involves three steps: placement, layering and integration.

notes.front: In money laundering, what is placement?
notes.back: The first step: illegitimate funds are secretly introduced into the legitimate financial system.
notes.explanation: FinCEN says laundering typically involves three steps, and placement comes first.
notes.example: Like slipping forged notes into a shop’s till among the real ones.
notes.source: FinCEN, History of Anti-Money Laundering Laws, “History of Anti-Money Laundering Laws”
notes.evidence: Typically, it involves three steps: placement, layering and integration. First, the illegitimate funds are furtively introduced into the legitimate financial system.

notes.front: In money laundering, what is layering?
notes.back: The second step: the money is moved around to create confusion, sometimes by wiring or transferring it through numerous accounts.
notes.explanation: FinCEN puts it after placement and before integration.
notes.example: Like shuffling cups so fast that no one can follow the coin.
notes.source: FinCEN, History of Anti-Money Laundering Laws, “History of Anti-Money Laundering Laws”
notes.evidence: Then, the money is moved around to create confusion, sometimes by wiring or transferring through numerous accounts. Finally, it is integrated into the financial system through additional transactions until the "dirty money" appears "clean."

notes.front: What is structuring?
notes.back: Conducting currency transactions in any manner, such as splitting a large sum, to evade the currency-transaction reporting requirements.
notes.explanation: The definition covers acting alone or with others, at one or more institutions, on one or more days.
notes.example: Like paying a big bill in many small instalments just to stay under a checking limit.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1010.100 (General definitions), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 1010.100(xx)”, p. 8
notes.evidence: a person structures a transaction if that person, acting alone, or in conjunction with, or on behalf of, other persons, conducts or attempts to conduct one or more transactions in currency, in any amount, at one or more financial institutions, on one or more days, in any manner, for the purpose of evading the reporting requirements

notes.front: What is an anti-money laundering (AML) program at a broker-dealer?
notes.back: A written programme reasonably designed to achieve and monitor the firm’s compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act and its regulations.
notes.explanation: The notice says Rule 3310 requires each member firm to develop and implement one, consistent with section 352 of the PATRIOT Act.
notes.example: Like a shop’s written plan against shoplifting, with staff, checks and training.
notes.source: SEC notice of FINRA rule change to Rule 3310 (AML compliance program), 83 FR (8 May 2018), “Purpose”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Consistent with Section 352 of the PATRIOT Act, and incorporating the four pillars, FINRA Rule 3310 requires each member firm to develop and implement a written AML program reasonably designed to achieve and monitor the member firm’s compliance with the BSA and implementing regulations.

notes.front: What is a customer identification program (CIP)?
notes.back: A broker-dealer’s written, documented programme for identifying its customers, which must form part of its AML programme.
notes.explanation: The regulation requires the programme to be written and appropriate for the firm’s size and business.
notes.example: Like a hotel checking your passport at check-in, but written down as firm-wide procedures.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.220 (Customer identification programs for broker-dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.220(a)(1)”
notes.evidence: A broker-dealer must establish, document, and maintain a written Customer Identification Program (“CIP”) appropriate for its size and business that, at a minimum, includes each of the requirements of paragraphs (a)(1) through (a)(5) of this section. The CIP must be a part of the broker-dealer's anti-money laundering compliance program

notes.front: What is the USA PATRIOT Act?
notes.back: The Uniting and Strengthening America by Providing Appropriate Tools Required to Intercept and Obstruct Terrorism Act of 2001.
notes.explanation: The short name is built from the words of the official title. Among much else, its section 352 requires financial institutions to have anti-money laundering programmes.
notes.example: Like a single law that added new locks to many doors of the financial system at once.
notes.source: FinCEN, USA PATRIOT Act, “USA PATRIOT Act”
notes.evidence: The official title of the USA PATRIOT Act is "Uniting and Strengthening America by Providing Appropriate Tools Required to Intercept and Obstruct Terrorism (USA PATRIOT) Act of 2001."

notes.front: What is a Suspicious Activity Report (SAR)?
notes.back: The report a broker-dealer completes to report a suspicious transaction, keeping supporting documentation.
notes.explanation: The regulation also requires the firm to collect and keep supporting documentation with the report.
notes.example: Like a bank teller’s private note to the police about an odd deposit.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.320 (Suspicious activity reports by brokers or dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.320(b)(1)”
notes.evidence: A suspicious transaction shall be reported by completing a Suspicious Activity Report (“SAR”), and collecting and maintaining supporting documentation

notes.front: What is a Currency Transaction Report (CTR)?
notes.back: A report a financial institution files on each deposit, withdrawal, exchange or transfer involving a transaction in currency of more than $10,000.
notes.explanation: The regulation applies it to each financial institution other than a casino.
notes.example: Like a till that rings an alarm whenever a very large cash payment passes over the counter.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1010.311 (Currency transaction reports), eCFR, “§ 1010.311”
notes.evidence: Each financial institution other than a casino shall file a report of each deposit, withdrawal, exchange of currency or other payment or transfer, by, through, or to such financial institution which involves a transaction in currency of more than $10,000

notes.front: What is the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN)?
notes.back: The federal body whose mission is to safeguard the financial system from illicit activity and counter money laundering and terrorist financing.
notes.explanation: Its mission statement says it does this by collecting, analysing and disseminating financial intelligence.
notes.example: Like a national lost-property office for suspicious money reports, which then helps investigators.
notes.source: FinCEN, Mission, “Mission”
notes.evidence: The mission of the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network is to safeguard the financial system from illicit activity, counter money laundering and the financing of terrorism, and promote national security through strategic use of financial authorities and the collection, analysis, and dissemination of financial intelligence.

notes.front: What is the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC)?
notes.back: The Treasury office that administers and enforces economic and trade sanctions against targeted jurisdictions, regimes, individuals and entities.
notes.explanation: Its targets include terrorists and international narcotics traffickers, among others.
notes.example: Like a border guard for money, turning away payments to blacklisted people.
notes.source: OFAC FAQs, Basic Information on OFAC and Sanctions, “FAQ 1”
notes.evidence: The U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) administers and enforces economic and trade sanctions against targeted foreign jurisdictions and regimes, as well as individuals and entities engaging in harmful activity, such as terrorists, international narcotics traffickers

notes.front: What is the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN list)?
notes.back: OFAC’s list of individuals, groups and entities, such as terrorists and narcotics traffickers, whose assets are blocked.
notes.explanation: OFAC says United States persons are generally prohibited from dealing with anyone on it.
notes.example: Like a “do not serve” list pinned behind a bar, but for money.
notes.source: OFAC FAQs, Specially Designated Nationals (SDNs) and the SDN List, “FAQ 18”
notes.evidence: It also lists individuals, groups, and entities, such as terrorists and narcotics traffickers designated under programs that are not country-specific. Collectively, such individuals and companies are called "Specially Designated Nationals" or "SDNs." Their assets are blocked and U.S. persons are generally prohibited from dealing with them.

notes.front: What is a confirmation?
notes.back: The written notification a broker-dealer gives or sends a customer, at or before completion of a transaction, disclosing its details.
notes.explanation: Rule 10b-10 exempts transactions in savings bonds and municipal securities from this requirement.
notes.example: Like a receipt for a purchase, but it must arrive by the time the deal completes.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.10b-10 (Confirmation of transactions), eCFR, “§ 240.10b-10(a)”
notes.evidence: any security (other than U.S. Savings Bonds or municipal securities) unless such broker or dealer, at or before completion of such transaction, gives or sends to such customer written notification disclosing

notes.front: What is an account statement?
notes.back: A periodic statement sent to the customer describing securities positions, money balances and account activity since the previous statement.
notes.explanation: Rule 2231 generally requires a general securities member to send one at least once each calendar quarter.
notes.example: Like a bank statement, but listing shares held as well as cash.
notes.source: SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rule 2231 (Customer Account Statements), 87 FR (7 June 2022), “Background”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Rule 2231 and NYSE Rule 409T generally require a general securities member 9 to, at least once each calendar quarter, send account statements to customers containing a description of any securities positions, money balances or account activity in the accounts since the prior account statements were sent

notes.front: What is a business continuity plan (BCP)?
notes.back: A firm’s written plan setting out procedures for an emergency or significant business disruption.
notes.explanation: The notice says the rule lists the minimum elements a plan must address, where applicable and necessary to the business.
notes.example: Like a school’s fire drill plan, but for keeping a brokerage running.
notes.source: SEC notice of FINRA proposal to adopt Rule 4370 (Business Continuity Plans and Emergency Contact Information), 74 FR (15 June 2009), “Purpose”, p. 2
notes.evidence: and maintain a written business continuity plan identifying procedures relating to an emergency or significant business disruption and enumerates the minimum elements that a member’s business continuity plan must address, to the extent those elements are applicable and necessary to the member’s business.
notes.validAsOf: 2009-06-15 · FINRA Rule 4370 as proposed in 2009; later amendments not checked

notes.front: What is Regulation S-P (Reg S-P)?
notes.back: The Securities and Exchange Commission’s regulation on the privacy of consumer financial information and the safeguarding of personal information.
notes.explanation: The subpart’s heading names both jobs: keeping consumer financial information private and keeping personal information safe.
notes.example: Like a doctor’s confidentiality code, but for a broker’s customer files.
notes.source: 17 CFR 248.1 (Regulation S-P purpose and scope), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 248.1(a)”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Subpart A—Regulation S-P: Privacy of Consumer Financial Information and Safeguarding Personal Information

notes.front: What is nonpublic personal information (NPI)?
notes.back: Personally identifiable financial information, and any list or grouping of consumers derived from such information that is not publicly available.
notes.explanation: The second limb means a customer list can be NPI if it was built from personally identifiable financial information.
notes.example: Like a customer’s account balance and trading history, not the name in a phone book.
notes.source: 17 CFR 248.3 (Regulation S-P definitions), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 248.3(t)”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Nonpublic personal information means: (i) Personally identifiable financial information; and (ii) Any list, description, or other grouping of consumers (and publicly available information pertaining to them) that is derived using any personally identifiable financial information that is not publicly available information.

notes.front: What is a privacy notice under Reg S-P?
notes.back: A clear and conspicuous notice that accurately reflects the firm’s privacy policies and practices.
notes.explanation: Accuracy is part of the test: the notice must reflect what the firm actually does with information.
notes.example: Like the privacy leaflet a bank hands you when you open an account.
notes.source: 17 CFR 248.4 (Initial privacy notice), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 248.4(a)”, p. 1
notes.evidence: You must provide a clear and conspicuous notice that accurately reflects your privacy policies and practices to

notes.front: What is a trusted contact person?
notes.back: A person you authorise your brokerage firm to contact in limited circumstances, such as when it cannot reach you or suspects financial exploitation.
notes.explanation: The two examples the glossary gives are trouble reaching the customer and a reasonable belief of possible financial exploitation.
notes.example: Like the emergency contact on a school form: someone to call, not someone who decides.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Trusted Contact”, “Trusted Contact”
notes.evidence: A trusted contact is a person that you authorize your brokerage firm to contact in limited circumstances, such as if your broker has trouble reaching you or has a reasonable belief that your account may be exposed to possible financial exploitation.

notes.front: Under the communications rule (Rule 2210), what are communications?
notes.back: A member firm’s communications with the public, divided into three categories: retail communications, correspondence and institutional communications.
notes.explanation: The approval order says the three categories matter because approval, filing and content standards apply differently to each.
notes.example: Like sorting post into letters, circulars and trade mailings, each with its own rules.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rule 2210 (Communications with the Public), 77 FR (4 April 2012), “III.A Categories of Communications”, p. 2
notes.evidence: The definitions of the three communication categories (‘‘institutional communications,’’ ‘‘retail communication,’’ and ‘‘correspondence’’) are important because the principal approval, filing and content standards apply differently to each category.
notes.validAsOf: 2012-04-04 · FINRA Rule 2210 as approved in 2012; later amendments not checked

notes.front: What is correspondence under Rule 2210?
notes.back: Any written (including electronic) communication distributed or made available to 25 or fewer retail investors within any 30-calendar-day period.
notes.explanation: The order contrasts it with a retail communication, which reaches more than 25 retail investors in that period.
notes.example: Like a personal letter or email to a handful of clients.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rule 2210 (Communications with the Public), 77 FR (4 April 2012), “III.A.1 Retail Communication and Correspondence”, p. 3
notes.evidence: FINRA proposed to define ‘‘retail communication’’ as ‘‘any written (including electronic) communication that is distributed or made available to more than 25 retail investors within any 30 calendar-day period’’ and ‘‘correspondence’’ as ‘‘any written (including electronic) communication that is distributed or made available to 25 or fewer retail investors within any 30 calendar-day period.’’
notes.validAsOf: 2012-04-04 · FINRA Rule 2210 as approved in 2012; later amendments not checked

notes.front: What is a retail communication under Rule 2210?
notes.back: Any written (including electronic) communication distributed or made available to more than 25 retail investors within any 30-calendar-day period.
notes.explanation: The count of retail investors reached in 30 days is what separates it from correspondence.
notes.example: Like a newsletter posted to hundreds of clients.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rule 2210 (Communications with the Public), 77 FR (4 April 2012), “III.A.1 Retail Communication and Correspondence”, p. 3
notes.evidence: FINRA proposed to define ‘‘retail communication’’ as ‘‘any written (including electronic) communication that is distributed or made available to more than 25 retail investors within any 30 calendar-day period’’
notes.validAsOf: 2012-04-04 · FINRA Rule 2210 as approved in 2012; later amendments not checked

notes.front: What is an institutional communication under Rule 2210?
notes.back: Any written (including electronic) communication distributed or made available only to institutional investors.
notes.explanation: Because it must go only to institutional investors, sending it to a retail investor takes it out of this category.
notes.example: Like a briefing handed only to pension-fund managers at a closed meeting.
notes.source: SEC notice of FINRA proposal to adopt Rule 2210 (Communications with the Public), 76 FR (3 August 2011), “Definitions of Institutional Communication and Institutional Investor”, p. 10
notes.evidence: The Notice proposal defined ‘‘institutional communication’’ as ‘‘any written (including electronic) communication that is distributed or made available only to institutional investors.’’
notes.validAsOf: 2012-04-04 · FINRA Rule 2210 as approved in 2012; later amendments not checked

notes.front: What is telemarketing?
notes.back: A plan, programme or campaign to induce the purchase of goods or services, or a charitable contribution, by telephone, involving more than one interstate call.
notes.explanation: The definition covers charitable appeals as well as sales, and needs more than one interstate call.
notes.example: Like a call-centre campaign ringing people to sell a product.
notes.source: 16 CFR 310.2 (Telemarketing Sales Rule definitions), CFR 2026 edition, “§ 310.2 “Telemarketing””, p. 4
notes.evidence: Telemarketing means a plan, program, or campaign which is conducted to induce the purchase of goods or services or a charitable contribution, by use of one or more telephones and which involves more than one interstate telephone call.

notes.front: What is a do-not-call list?
notes.back: A list of people who do not want telephone solicitations, which telemarketing rules require member firms to maintain.
notes.explanation: The order says both older telemarketing rules required members to maintain do-not-call lists and limit calling hours.
notes.example: Like a “no junk mail” sticker on a letterbox, but for phone calls.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3230 (Telemarketing), 77 FR (3 February 2012), “II. Description of the Proposal”, p. 1
notes.evidence: NASD Rule 2212 and NYSE Rule 440A are similar rules that require members to maintain do-not-call lists, limit the hours of telephone solicitations and prohibit members from using deceptive and abusive acts and practices in connection with telemarketing.
notes.validAsOf: 2012-02-03 · FINRA Rule 3230 as approved in 2012; later amendments not checked

notes.front: What is the Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR)?
notes.back: The Federal Trade Commission’s telemarketing rule, under which a firm-specific do-not-call request must be honoured indefinitely.
notes.explanation: The notice says the securities rule’s old five-year period was dropped to match it.
notes.example: Like a national highway code that local roads must copy.
notes.source: SEC notice of FINRA proposal to adopt Rule 3230 (Telemarketing), 76 FR (2 November 2011), “Firm-specific do-not-call requests”, p. 2
notes.evidence: because the time for which the firmspecific opt-out must be honored under the FTC’s Telemarketing Sales Rule 17 is indefinite, rather than five years as currently provided in the rule.

notes.front: What is Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI)?
notes.back: The rule requiring a broker-dealer recommending a securities transaction or strategy to a retail customer to act in that customer’s best interest.
notes.explanation: The rule forbids putting the firm’s or representative’s own interest ahead of the customer’s when recommending.
notes.example: Like a doctor who must prescribe what suits the patient, not what pays best.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15l-1 (Regulation Best Interest), eCFR, “§ 240.15l-1(a)(1)”
notes.evidence: shall act in the best interest of the retail customer at the time the recommendation is made, without placing the financial or other interest of the broker, dealer, or natural person who is an associated person of a broker or dealer making the recommendation ahead of the interest of the retail customer.

notes.front: In Reg BI and suitability, what is a recommendation?
notes.back: Advice to a customer to make a securities transaction or follow an investment strategy involving securities, including advice about account type.
notes.explanation: Reg BI’s wording expressly includes account recommendations, not only trades.
notes.example: Like a waiter saying “order the fish”, as opposed to handing you the menu.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15l-1 (Regulation Best Interest), eCFR, “§ 240.15l-1(a)(1)”
notes.evidence: when making a recommendation of any securities transaction or investment strategy involving securities (including account recommendations) to a retail customer

notes.front: What is Form CRS?
notes.back: A client or customer relationship summary that advisers and brokers must deliver when starting a relationship or when the account changes.
notes.explanation: The glossary’s example of an account change is rolling over an IRA.
notes.example: Like a menu board listing a restaurant’s services and prices before you sit down.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Form CRS”, “Form CRS”
notes.evidence: Form CRS is a client or customer relationship summary. Advisers and brokers are required to deliver a relationship summary to you when starting a relationship with you or when your account changes (e.g., you rollover an IRA).

notes.front: What is the know your customer (KYC) obligation (Rule 2090)?
notes.back: A duty to use reasonable diligence, in opening and maintaining every account, to know and retain the essential facts about every customer.
notes.explanation: The order says the duty starts with the relationship and does not depend on any recommendation.
notes.example: Like a family doctor keeping an up-to-date file on each patient.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rules 2090 (Know Your Customer) and 2111 (Suitability), 75 FR 71479 (23 November 2010), “A. Proposed FINRA Rule 2090”, p. 2
notes.evidence: the rule would require broker-dealers to use ‘‘reasonable diligence,’’ with regard to the opening and maintenance of every account, in order to know and retain the essential facts concerning every customer.8 The obligation would arise at the beginning of the customer/broker relationship, independent of whether the broker has made a recommendation

notes.front: What is reasonable-basis suitability?
notes.back: Having reasonable grounds, based on reasonable diligence, to believe a recommendation is suitable for at least some investors.
notes.explanation: It asks about the product or strategy in general, before any particular customer is considered.
notes.example: Like a chef tasting a new dish before putting it on the menu for anyone.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rules 2090 (Know Your Customer) and 2111 (Suitability), 75 FR 71479 (23 November 2010), “B. Proposed FINRA Rule 2111”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Reasonable basis (members must have reasonable grounds to believe, based on reasonable diligence, that a recommendation is suitable for at least some investors)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rule 2111 as amended in 2020: applies only where Reg BI does not

notes.front: What is customer-specific suitability?
notes.back: Having reasonable grounds to believe a recommendation is suitable for the particular investor at issue.
notes.explanation: Where reasonable-basis suitability asks about some investors, this obligation asks about the one being advised.
notes.example: Like a tailor fitting a suit to one person rather than selling a standard size.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rules 2090 (Know Your Customer) and 2111 (Suitability), 75 FR 71479 (23 November 2010), “B. Proposed FINRA Rule 2111”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Customer specific (members must have reasonable grounds to believe a recommendation is suitable for the particular investor at issue)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rule 2111 as amended in 2020: applies only where Reg BI does not

notes.front: What is quantitative suitability?
notes.back: Having a reasonable basis to believe the number of transactions recommended to a customer within a certain period is not excessive.
notes.explanation: It looks at a series of recommendations together, not at any single trade. Since 2020 FINRA no longer has to prove that the firm controlled the account.
notes.example: Like a doctor checking that the total dose over a week is safe, not only each pill.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rules 2090 (Know Your Customer) and 2111 (Suitability), 75 FR 71479 (23 November 2010), “B. Proposed FINRA Rule 2111”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Quantitative (members must have a reasonable basis to believe the number of transactions recommended to a customer within a certain period is not excessive)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rule 2111 as amended in 2020: applies only where Reg BI does not

notes.front: In a cash account, what can happen if an investor buys and sells a security before paying for it (freeriding)?
notes.back: Reg T does not permit it, and the broker may have to freeze the cash account for 90 days.
notes.explanation: The glossary calls buying and selling before payment “freeriding”, and that is what can trigger the freeze.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Cash Account”, “Cash Account”
notes.evidence: If an investor buys and sells a security before paying for it, the investor is “freeriding” which is not permitted under Regulation T and may require the investor’s broker to “freeze” the investor’s cash account for 90 days.

notes.front: Under Reg T, a creditor must obtain full cash payment for a customer’s purchase of a nonexempted security in a cash account within {{c1::one payment period}} of the purchase date.
notes.explanation: The rule counts the time from the date the security was purchased.
notes.source: 12 CFR 220.8 (Regulation T cash account), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 220.8(b)(1)”, p. 1
notes.evidence: A creditor shall obtain full cash payment for customer purchases: (i) Within one payment period of the date: (A) Any nonexempted security was purchased;

notes.front: How does Reg T define the payment period?
notes.back: The number of business days in the standard securities settlement cycle, plus two business days.
notes.explanation: The definition ties the period to the settlement cycle defined in Rule 15c6-1(a).
notes.source: 12 CFR 220.2 (Regulation T definitions), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 220.2 “Payment period””, p. 3
notes.evidence: Payment period means the number of business days in the standard securities settlement cycle in the United States, as defined in paragraph (a) of SEC Rule 15c6–1 (17 CFR 240.15c6–1(a)), plus two business days.

notes.front: Under Reg T, the required margin for a margin equity security is {{c1::50 percent}} of its current market value, or the percentage set where the trade occurs if greater.
notes.explanation: The supplement applies the higher of the two figures.
notes.source: 12 CFR 220.12 (Regulation T), eCFR, “§ 220.12(a)”
notes.evidence: Margin equity security, except for an exempted security, money market mutual fund or exempted securities mutual fund, warrant on a securities index or foreign currency or a long position in an option: 50 percent of the current market value of the security or the percentage set by the regulatory authority where the trade occurs, whichever is greater.

notes.front: Before trading on margin, what minimum deposit do the self-regulator’s rules require?
notes.back: $2,000 or 100 percent of the purchase price of the margin securities, whichever is less.
notes.explanation: The bulletin calls this the minimum margin and notes some firms require more than $2,000.
notes.source: SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy, Investor Bulletin: Understanding Margin Accounts, “Minimum margin”
notes.evidence: requires you to deposit with your brokerage firm a minimum of $2,000 or 100 percent of the purchase price of the margin securities, whichever is less. This is known as the “minimum margin.” Some firms may require you to deposit more than $2,000.

notes.front: The self-regulator’s rules require the maintenance requirement to be at least {{c1::25 percent}} of the total market value of the margin securities.
notes.explanation: The bulletin adds that many firms set higher house requirements, typically 30 to 40 percent.
notes.source: SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy, Investor Bulletin: Understanding Margin Accounts, “Maintenance requirements”
notes.evidence: FINRA rules require this “maintenance requirement” to be at least 25 percent of the total market value of the margin securities. However, many brokerage firms have higher maintenance requirements, typically between 30 to 40 percent

notes.front: If margined securities fall in value, must the firm tell the customer before selling securities to cover the shortfall?
notes.back: No. It can demand an immediate deposit or sell securities in the account without informing the customer in advance.
notes.explanation: The glossary adds that the firm, not the customer, decides which securities to sell.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Margin Call”, “Margin Call”
notes.evidence: your brokerage firm can require you to deposit cash or securities to your account immediately, or sell any of the securities in your account to cover any shortfall, without informing you in advance. The brokerage firm decides which of your securities to sell.

notes.front: Under Reg T, a margin call must be satisfied within {{c1::one payment period}} after the margin deficiency was created or increased.
notes.explanation: The regulation allows the period to be extended for one or more limited periods.
notes.source: 12 CFR 220.4 (Regulation T margin account), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 220.4(c)(3)”, p. 2
notes.evidence: (3) Time limits. (i) A margin call shall be satisfied within one payment period after the margin deficiency was created or increased. (ii) The payment period may be extended for one or more limited periods

notes.front: What must a customer sign to open a margin account?
notes.back: A margin agreement, which may be part of the general account-opening agreement or a separate document.
notes.explanation: The agreement states that the customer must abide by margin requirements set by the Federal Reserve Board and self-regulators, among others.
notes.source: SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy, Investor Bulletin: Understanding Margin Accounts, “Margin agreement”
notes.evidence: To open a margin account, your broker will have you sign a margin agreement. The margin agreement may be part of your general brokerage account opening agreement or may be a separate agreement. The margin agreement states that you must abide by the margin requirements established by the Federal Reserve Board, self-regulatory organizations (SROs) such as FINRA

notes.front: When must a firm give a non-institutional customer the margin disclosure statement (Rule 2264)?
notes.back: Prior to or at the time of opening the margin account.
notes.explanation: The notice says the statement highlights the risks of trading securities in a margin account.
notes.source: SEC notice of FINRA proposal to adopt Rule 2264 (Margin Disclosure Statement), 74 FR (11 August 2009), “Purpose”, p. 1
notes.evidence: to deliver to such customers, prior to or at the time of opening the account, a specified margin disclosure statement to highlight the risks involved in trading securities in a margin account.
notes.validAsOf: 2009-08-11 · FINRA Rule 2264 as proposed in 2009; later amendments not checked

notes.front: For options trading, what do brokerage firms generally require, and may the customer buy options on margin?
notes.back: Generally a margin account; but firms do not let customers use margin to buy options contracts.
notes.explanation: The bulletin says firms may let customers use margin to sell (write) options instead.
notes.source: SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy, Investor Bulletin: Understanding Margin Accounts, “Options and margin”
notes.evidence: Brokerage firms generally require you to have a margin account to trade options, but they do not allow you to use margin to purchase options contracts. However, brokerage firms may allow you to use margin to sell (or write) options contracts.

notes.front: Before accepting a customer’s options order or approving the account for options, what must a broker-dealer have furnished?
notes.back: A copy of the definitive options disclosure document for that options class.
notes.explanation: Rule 9b-1 bars both the order and the account approval until the document has been furnished.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.9b-1 (Options disclosure document), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 240.9b-1(d)(1)”, p. 2
notes.evidence: shall accept an order from a customer to purchase or sell an option contract relating to an options class that is the subject of a definitive options disclosure document, or approve the customer’s account for the trading of such option, unless the broker or dealer furnishes or has furnished to the customer a copy of the definitive options disclosure document.

notes.front: Under Exchange Act section 11(d), when may a broker-dealer not extend credit to a customer on a new-issue security?
notes.back: When it participated in the distribution as a selling syndicate or group member within the previous thirty days.
notes.explanation: It covers maintaining or arranging credit as well as extending it.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. 78k (Exchange Act s. 11), “§ 78k(d)(1)”
notes.evidence: he extends or maintains or arranges for the extension or maintenance of credit to or for a customer on any security (other than an exempted security) which was a part of a new issue in the distribution of which he participated as a member of a selling syndicate or group within thirty days prior to such transaction

notes.front: In a discretionary account, what kind of trading does Rule 15c1-7 treat as a manipulative, deceptive or fraudulent device?
notes.back: Transactions excessive in size or frequency in view of the account’s financial resources and character.
notes.explanation: The rule applies wherever the broker or its agent or employee is vested with discretionary power over the account.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15c1-7 (Discretionary accounts), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 240.15c1-7(a)”, p. 1
notes.evidence: is vested with any discretionary power any transactions or purchase or sale which are excessive in size or frequency in view of the financial resources and character of such account.

notes.front: Under Rule 15c1-7, what record must be made immediately after each discretionary transaction?
notes.back: One showing the customer’s name; the security’s name, amount and price; and the date and time of the transaction.
notes.explanation: Timing matters: the rule requires the record immediately after effecting the transaction.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15c1-7 (Discretionary accounts), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 240.15c1-7(b)”, p. 1
notes.evidence: unless immediately after effecting such transaction such broker, dealer or municipal securities dealer makes a record of such transaction which record includes the name of such customer, the name, amount and price of the security, and the date and time when such transaction took place.

notes.front: A wrap account’s fee or fees are generally based on {{c1::the total market value of the account}}.
notes.explanation: The glossary ties the fee to the account’s total market value.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Wrap Account”, “Wrap Account”
notes.evidence: The fee or fees are generally based on the total market value of the investment account.

notes.front: What does a commission compensate, and in what capacity is the firm acting?
notes.back: It compensates the financial professional and firm when the firm acts as agent for the customer in the securities transaction.
notes.explanation: The glossary says you will likely pay one when buying or selling securities through a financial professional.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Commissions”, “Commissions”
notes.evidence: You will likely pay a commission when you buy or sell stock or other securities, such as mutual fund or ETF shares, through a financial professional. The commission compensates the financial professional and his or her firm when it is acting as agent for you in your securities transaction.

notes.front: What is an education savings plan, and what can it pay for?
notes.back: A type of 529 plan; it saves for the beneficiary’s qualified higher education expenses, school tuition and certain other education costs.
notes.explanation: The glossary includes elementary and secondary school tuition at public, private or religious schools.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Education Savings Plan”, “Education Savings Plan”
notes.evidence: A type of 529 plan that lets an account owner open an investment account to save for the account beneficiary’s qualified higher education expenses , tuition and certain expenses for elementary or secondary public, private, or religious schools, and certain other education-related expenses.

notes.front: For a joint account, whose personal information must the account record include, and may financial information be combined?
notes.back: Each joint owner who is a natural person; their financial information may be combined.
notes.explanation: Rule 17a-3 separates personal details, kept per owner, from financial details, which can be pooled.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-3 (Records to be made), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 240.17a-3(a)(17)(i)(A)”, p. 7
notes.evidence: In the case of a joint account, the account record must include personal information for each joint owner who is a natural person; however, financial information for the individual joint owners may be combined.
uses: joint tenants with right of survivorship

notes.front: What typically happens to a formal revocable trust when its owner dies?
notes.back: It typically becomes irrevocable, with deposits paid to the identified beneficiaries.
notes.explanation: On the owner’s death the deposits go to the identified beneficiaries.
notes.source: FDIC, Your Insured Deposits, “Trust Accounts”
notes.evidence: The agreement establishes that the deposits are to be paid to one or more identified beneficiaries upon the owner’s death. These trusts typically become irrevocable upon the owner’s death.

notes.front: Can a donor take back property transferred to a minor under UTMA?
notes.back: No. Under UTMA the donor makes an irrevocable transfer of money or other property to the minor.
notes.explanation: The manual’s word is irrevocable: the gift cannot be revoked.
notes.source: Social Security POMS SI 01120.205, Uniform Transfers to Minors Act, “C. UTMA provisions”
notes.evidence: a donor makes an irrevocable transfer of money or other property to a minor;

notes.front: Under UTMA, the transfer and any income it generates stay under a custodian’s control until the minor reaches {{c1::the age of majority established by state law}}.
notes.explanation: The age is whatever state law sets.
notes.source: Social Security POMS SI 01120.205, Uniform Transfers to Minors Act, “C. UTMA provisions”
notes.evidence: the transfer, plus any income it generates, is under the control of a custodian until the minor reaches the age of majority established by State law;

notes.front: Under UTMA, how much of the assets may the custodian spend for the minor?
notes.back: As much as the custodian deems equitable, provided to the minor or spent for the minor’s use and benefit.
notes.explanation: The spending must be for the minor, not for the custodian.
notes.source: Social Security POMS SI 01120.205, Uniform Transfers to Minors Act, “C. UTMA provisions”
notes.evidence: the custodian has discretion to provide to the minor or spend for the minor's use and benefit as much of the assets as they deem equitable; and

notes.front: For 2026, what is the most a person can contribute in total to all their traditional and Roth IRAs?
notes.back: $7,500, or $8,600 if age 50 or older (or taxable compensation, if less).
notes.explanation: The limit is shared across all of a person’s traditional and Roth IRAs, not set per account.
notes.source: IRS, Retirement topics: IRA contribution limits, “Contribution limits”
notes.evidence: For 2026, the total contributions you make each year to all of your traditional IRAs and Roth IRAs can’t be more than: $7,500 ($8,600 if you’re age 50 or older), or If less, your taxable compensation for the year
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: Are contributions to a traditional IRA deductible, and when are its earnings taxed?
notes.back: They may be fully or partially deductible, depending on filing status and income; amounts are generally not taxed until withdrawn.
notes.explanation: The tax authority says this applies to earnings and gains as well as contributions.
notes.source: IRS, Traditional IRAs, “Traditional IRAs”
notes.evidence: Contributions you make to a traditional IRA may be fully or partially deductible, depending on your filing status and income, and - Generally, amounts in your traditional IRA (including earnings and gains) are not taxed until you take a distribution (withdrawal) from your IRA.

notes.front: What can limit how much a person may contribute to a Roth IRA, beyond the combined IRA limit?
notes.back: Their filing status and income (modified adjusted gross income).
notes.explanation: The same combined contribution limit also applies across all Roth and traditional IRAs.
notes.source: IRS, Roth IRAs, “Roth IRAs”
notes.evidence: The same combined contribution limit applies to all of your Roth and traditional IRAs. Limits on Roth IRA contributions based on modified AGI Your Roth IRA contribution might be limited based on your filing status and income.

notes.front: When must withdrawals be taken from a Roth IRA?
notes.back: Not until after the account owner’s death; beneficiaries are then subject to the RMD rules.
notes.explanation: The same applies to designated Roth accounts in 401(k) and 403(b) plans.
notes.source: IRS, Retirement plan and IRA required minimum distributions FAQs, “RMD rules”
notes.evidence: Withdrawals from Roth IRAs and Designated Roth accounts (401(k) or 403(b)) are not required until after the death of the account owner. However, beneficiaries of Roth IRAs and Designated Roth accounts are subject to RMD rules.

notes.front: In a traditional 401(k) plan, when are contributions and earnings taxed?
notes.back: Not until they are withdrawn.
notes.explanation: Contributions come from pre-tax salary, so tax is deferred until withdrawal.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “401(k) Plan”, “401(k) Plan”
notes.evidence: Employees who participate in a traditional 401(k) plan have a portion of their pre-tax salary invested directly in the option or options they choose. These contributions and any earnings from the 401(k) investments are not taxed until they are withdrawn.

notes.front: Retirement plan participants and IRA owners generally must take RMDs annually starting with the year they reach age {{c1::73}}.
notes.explanation: The word “generally” matters: some plan participants may delay, as a later card shows.
notes.source: IRS, Retirement plan and IRA required minimum distributions FAQs, “RMD rules”
notes.evidence: account owners generally must withdraw annually starting with the year they reach age 73.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: Until when can the first RMD be delayed, and what does that mean for the second?
notes.back: Until 1 April of the year after reaching 73; the second RMD is still due by 31 December of that same year.
notes.explanation: The tax authority’s example: age 73 in 2024 means the first by 1 April 2025 and the second by 31 December 2025.
notes.source: IRS, Retirement plan and IRA required minimum distributions FAQs, “Q3”
notes.evidence: If you reach age 73 in 2024, you must take your first RMD by April 1, 2025, and the second RMD by Dec. 31, 2025.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: Who can delay RMDs until the year they retire, and who must start at 73 even if still working?
notes.back: Retirement plan owners, unless 5% owners of the sponsor, can delay; traditional IRA owners must start at 73.
notes.explanation: The tax authority applies the same must-start rule to owners of employer-linked IRAs.
notes.source: IRS, Retirement plan and IRA required minimum distributions FAQs, “RMD rules”
notes.evidence: Retirement plan account owners can delay taking their RMDs until the year in which they retire, unless they're a 5% owner of the business sponsoring the plan. Owners of traditional IRA, and SEP and SIMPLE IRA accounts must begin taking RMDs once the account holder is age 73, even if they're retired.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: What tax may apply if an account owner fails to withdraw the full RMD on time?
notes.back: An excise tax of 25% of the amount not withdrawn, or 10% if the RMD is timely corrected within two years.
notes.explanation: The tax authority says the owner reports it on Form 5329 with the federal return.
notes.source: IRS, Retirement plan and IRA required minimum distributions FAQs, “Q8”
notes.evidence: If an account owner fails to withdraw the full amount of the RMD by the due date, the amount not withdrawn may be subject to an excise tax of 25%, 10% if the RMD is timely corrected within two years. The account owner should file Form 5329
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: In FinCEN’s description, what is the third and final step of money laundering, after placement and layering?
notes.back: Integration: the money is integrated into the financial system through additional transactions until it appears clean.
notes.explanation: Integration completes the process that placement began.
notes.source: FinCEN, History of Anti-Money Laundering Laws, “History of Anti-Money Laundering Laws”
notes.evidence: Finally, it is integrated into the financial system through additional transactions until the "dirty money" appears "clean."

notes.front: Must a structured transaction exceed $10,000 at a single institution on a single day to count as structuring?
notes.back: No. Breaking a sum over $10,000 into smaller sums, at or below $10,000, can be structuring.
notes.explanation: Smaller sums at or below $10,000 are exactly what the definition describes.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1010.100 (General definitions), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 1010.100(xx)”, p. 8
notes.evidence: the breaking down of a single sum of currency exceeding $10,000 into smaller sums, including sums at or below $10,000, or the conduct of a transaction, or series of currency transactions at or below $10,000. The transaction or transactions need not exceed the $10,000 reporting threshold at any single financial institution on any single day

notes.front: What must a member’s AML programme establish so that suspicious transactions are caught?
notes.back: Policies and procedures that can be reasonably expected to detect and cause the reporting of suspicious transactions.
notes.explanation: The notice lists this first among the minimum elements of the programme.
notes.source: SEC notice of FINRA rule change to Rule 3310 (AML compliance program), 83 FR (8 May 2018), “Purpose”, p. 2
notes.evidence: FINRA Rule 3310 requires that each member firm, at a minimum: (1) Establish and implement policies and procedures that can be reasonably expected to detect and cause the reporting of suspicious transactions;

notes.front: How often must a member’s AML programme be independently tested, and by whom?
notes.back: Annually (on a calendar-year basis), by member firm personnel or a qualified outside party.
notes.explanation: The notice lists this as the third minimum element.
notes.source: SEC notice of FINRA rule change to Rule 3310 (AML compliance program), 83 FR (8 May 2018), “Purpose”, p. 2
notes.evidence: (3) provide for annual (on a calendar-year basis) independent testing for compliance to be conducted by member firm personnel

notes.front: Who must a member designate for its AML programme, and whom must it tell?
notes.back: An AML compliance person (or persons) for day-to-day operations and internal controls, identified to the self-regulator, with prompt notice of changes.
notes.explanation: The notice lists this as the fourth minimum element.
notes.source: SEC notice of FINRA rule change to Rule 3310 (AML compliance program), 83 FR (8 May 2018), “Purpose”, p. 2
notes.evidence: (4) designate and identify to FINRA an individual or individuals (i.e., AML compliance person(s)) who will be responsible for implementing and monitoring the day-to-day operations and internal controls of the AML program and provide prompt notification to FINRA of any changes to the designation;

notes.front: What must a member’s AML programme provide for its staff?
notes.back: Ongoing training for appropriate persons.
notes.explanation: The notice lists training as the fifth minimum element.
notes.source: SEC notice of FINRA rule change to Rule 3310 (AML compliance program), 83 FR (8 May 2018), “Purpose”, p. 2
notes.evidence: and provide prompt notification to FINRA of any changes to the designation; and (5) provide ongoing training for appropriate persons.

notes.front: Which section of the USA PATRIOT Act requires financial institutions to have AML programmes, and what must they include at a minimum?
notes.back: Section 352: internal policies, procedures and controls; a compliance officer; ongoing employee training; and an independent audit.
notes.explanation: FinCEN summarises the section in these four elements.
notes.source: FinCEN, USA PATRIOT Act, “Section 352”
notes.evidence: Section 352: Anti-Money Laundering Programs Requires financial institutions to establish anti-money laundering programs, which at a minimum must include: the development of internal policies, procedures and controls; designation of a compliance officer; an ongoing employee training program; and an independent audit function to test programs.

notes.front: Which three items does the CIP rule list first among the minimum information to obtain before opening an account?
notes.back: Name; date of birth (for an individual); and address.
notes.explanation: The rule requires these before the account is opened, not afterwards.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.220 (Customer identification programs for broker-dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.220(a)(2)(i)(A)”
notes.evidence: the broker-dealer must obtain, at a minimum, the following information prior to opening an account: ( 1 ) Name; ( 2 ) Date of birth, for an individual; ( 3 ) Address, which shall be:

notes.front: What identification number must a CIP obtain from a United States person before opening an account?
notes.back: A taxpayer identification number.
notes.explanation: For a non-United States person, a passport number or similar number may be used instead.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.220 (Customer identification programs for broker-dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.220(a)(2)(i)(A)(4)”
notes.evidence: Identification number, which shall be: ( i ) For a U.S. person, a taxpayer identification number; or ( ii ) for a non-U.S. person, one or more of the following: A taxpayer identification number, a passport number and country of issuance

notes.front: A CIP must verify each customer’s identity {{c1::within a reasonable time before or after}} the account is opened.
notes.explanation: Collection of the information comes before opening; verification may follow within a reasonable time.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.220 (Customer identification programs for broker-dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.220(a)(2)(ii)”
notes.evidence: The CIP must contain procedures for verifying the identity of each customer, using information obtained in accordance with paragraph (a)(2)(i) of this section, within a reasonable time before or after the customer's account is opened.

notes.front: Which government lists must CIP procedures check customers against?
notes.back: Any federal list of known or suspected terrorists or terrorist organisations that the Treasury designates.
notes.explanation: Both kinds of listed party count: terrorists and terrorist organisations, known or suspected.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.220 (Customer identification programs for broker-dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.220(a)(4)”
notes.evidence: The CIP must include procedures for determining whether a customer appears on any list of known or suspected terrorists or terrorist organizations issued by any Federal government agency and designated as such by Treasury

notes.front: Identifying information obtained under a CIP must be kept for {{c1::five years after the account is closed}}.
notes.explanation: Other CIP records are kept five years after they are made.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.220 (Customer identification programs for broker-dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.220(a)(3)”
notes.evidence: for five years after the account is closed and the records made under paragraphs (a)(3)(i)(B), (C) and (D) of this section for five years after the record is made.

notes.front: Under section 314(a) information sharing, what may FinCEN require a financial institution to do?
notes.back: Search its records for accounts held for, or transactions with, specified individuals, entities or organisations.
notes.explanation: The search covers past as well as current accounts and transactions.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1010.520 (Information sharing between government agencies and financial institutions), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 1010.520(b)”, p. 2
notes.evidence: FinCEN may require any financial institution to search its records to determine whether the financial institution maintains or has maintained accounts for, or has engaged in transactions with, any specified individual, entity, or organization.

notes.front: A broker-dealer must file a SAR on a suspicious transaction that involves or aggregates funds or other assets of at least {{c1::$5,000}}.
notes.explanation: The broker-dealer must also know, suspect or have reason to suspect the transaction.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.320 (Suspicious activity reports by brokers or dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.320(a)(2)”
notes.evidence: it involves or aggregates funds or other assets of at least $5,000, and the broker-dealer knows, suspects, or has reason to suspect that the transaction

notes.front: A SAR must be filed no later than {{c1::30 calendar days}} after the broker-dealer’s initial detection of facts that may be a basis for filing.
notes.explanation: The clock starts at initial detection, not at the transaction.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.320 (Suspicious activity reports by brokers or dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.320(b)(3)”
notes.evidence: A SAR shall be filed no later than 30 calendar days after the date of the initial detection by the reporting broker-dealer

notes.front: If no suspect is identified on the date of initial detection, how long may SAR filing be delayed?
notes.back: An additional 30 calendar days, but never more than 60 calendar days after initial detection.
notes.explanation: The extra time is to identify a suspect.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.320 (Suspicious activity reports by brokers or dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.320(b)(3)”
notes.evidence: If no suspect is identified on the date of such initial detection, a broker-dealer may delay filing a SAR for an additional 30 calendar days to identify a suspect, but in no case shall reporting be delayed more than 60 calendar days after the date of such initial detection.

notes.front: For violations needing immediate attention, such as terrorist financing, what must a broker-dealer do besides filing a SAR on time?
notes.back: Immediately notify an appropriate law enforcement authority by telephone.
notes.explanation: The regulation gives ongoing money laundering schemes as another example.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.320 (Suspicious activity reports by brokers or dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.320(b)(3)”
notes.evidence: In situations involving violations that require immediate attention, such as terrorist financing or ongoing money laundering schemes, the broker-dealer shall immediately notify by telephone an appropriate law enforcement authority in addition to filing timely a SAR.

notes.front: May a broker-dealer employee tell anyone that a SAR has been filed?
notes.back: No: no broker-dealer or its director, officer, employee or agent may disclose a SAR or information revealing one, except as authorised.
notes.explanation: The regulation makes both the report and anything revealing its existence confidential.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.320 (Suspicious activity reports by brokers or dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.320(e)(1)(i)”
notes.evidence: No broker-dealer, and no director, officer, employee, or agent of any broker-dealer, shall disclose a SAR or any information that would reveal the existence of a SAR.

notes.front: A financial institution must file a report on each transaction in currency of {{c1::more than $10,000}}.
notes.explanation: The threshold is “more than”, so exactly $10,000 does not reach it.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1010.311 (Currency transaction reports), eCFR, “§ 1010.311”
notes.evidence: which involves a transaction in currency of more than $10,000

notes.front: Who must comply with OFAC sanctions?
notes.back: All United States persons: citizens and permanent residents wherever located, everyone within the country, and domestic companies with their foreign branches.
notes.explanation: Location does not matter for citizens and permanent residents.
notes.source: OFAC FAQs, Basic Information on OFAC and Sanctions, “FAQ 11”
notes.evidence: All U.S. persons must comply with OFAC sanctions, including all U.S. citizens and permanent residents regardless of where they are located, all individuals and entities within the United States, and all U.S. incorporated entities and their foreign branches.

notes.front: A report of property blocked under OFAC sanctions must be filed within {{c1::10 business days}} of the date the property becomes blocked.
notes.explanation: The clock runs in business days from the date of blocking.
notes.source: 31 CFR 501.603 (Reports of blocked property), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 501.603(b)(1)”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Reports shall be filed within 10 business days from the date that property becomes blocked.

notes.front: Does OFAC itself seize blocked funds?
notes.back: No. Financial institutions block (“freeze”) the property in their possession and report it to OFAC.
notes.explanation: Funds, accounts and other property in the institution’s possession or control can all be blocked.
notes.source: OFAC FAQs, OFAC Licenses, “FAQ 51”
notes.evidence: OFAC itself does not seize or hold blocked funds. To comply with U.S. sanctions regulations administered by OFAC, U.S. financial institutions are required to block or "freeze" certain property (e.g., funds, accounts) in their possession or control and report such blocked property to OFAC.

notes.front: How long must blotters, ledgers and similar records under Rule 17a-3(a)(1)–(3) be kept?
notes.back: At least six years, the first two in an easily accessible place.
notes.explanation: Records under Rule 17a-3(a)(5), (21) and (22) share the same six-year period.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-4 (Records to be preserved), eCFR, “§ 240.17a-4(a)”
notes.evidence: must preserve for a period of not less than 6 years, the first two years in an easily accessible place, all records required to be made pursuant to § 240.17a-3(a)(1) through (3), (5), and (21) and (22)

notes.front: How long must records of the terms and conditions for opening and maintaining a customer’s account be kept?
notes.back: At least six years after the customer’s account is closed.
notes.explanation: The clock starts at closing, not at opening.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-4 (Records to be preserved), eCFR, “§ 240.17a-4(c)”
notes.evidence: must preserve for a period of not less than six years after the closing of any customer's account any account cards or records which relate to the terms and conditions with respect to the opening and maintenance of the account.

notes.front: How long must order memoranda, complaint records and similar records under Rule 17a-3(a)(6)–(11) and (18)–(20) be kept?
notes.back: At least three years, the first two in an easily accessible place.
notes.explanation: Records under Rule 17a-3(a)(4), (16) and (25) to (31) share the same three-year period.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-4 (Records to be preserved), eCFR, “§ 240.17a-4(b)”
notes.evidence: must preserve for a period of not less than three years, the first two years in an easily accessible place: (1) All records required to be made pursuant to § 240.17a-3(a)(4), (6) through (11), (16), (18) through (20), and (25) through (31)

notes.front: For both six-year and three-year records under Rule 17a-4, the first {{c1::two years}} must be kept in an easily accessible place.
notes.explanation: The accessibility period is the same whichever retention period applies.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-4 (Records to be preserved), eCFR, “§ 240.17a-4(a) and (b)”
