notes.evidence: must preserve for a period of not less than three years, the first two years in an easily accessible place:

notes.front: Under Rule 17a-3, must a firm keep a memorandum of a brokerage order that was never executed?
notes.back: Yes: a memorandum is required for each brokerage order, executed or unexecuted.
notes.explanation: An order that was cancelled or never filled still leaves a record.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-3 (Records to be made), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 240.17a-3(a)(6)(i)”, p. 3
notes.evidence: A memorandum of each brokerage order, and of any other instruction, given or received for the purchase or sale of a security, except for the purchase or sale of a security-based swap, whether executed or unexecuted.

notes.front: For a natural-person customer, what are three items the account record must include?
notes.back: Any three of: name, tax identification number, address, telephone number, date of birth, employment status, annual income, net worth, investment objectives.
notes.explanation: Employment status includes occupation and whether the customer is an associated person of a broker-dealer.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-3 (Records to be made), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 240.17a-3(a)(17)(i)(A)”, p. 7
notes.evidence: An account record including the customer’s or owner’s name, tax identification number, address, telephone number, date of birth, employment status (including occupation and whether the customer is an associated person of a member, broker or dealer), annual income, net worth (excluding value of primary residence), and the account’s investment objectives.

notes.front: Who must sign and approve a customer’s account record?
notes.back: It must show whether it was signed by the associated person responsible for the account and approved or accepted by a principal.
notes.explanation: The record itself must indicate both steps.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-3 (Records to be made), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 240.17a-3(a)(17)(i)(A)”, p. 7
notes.evidence: The account record must indicate whether it has been signed by the associated person responsible for the account, if any, and approved or accepted by a principal of the member, broker or dealer.

notes.front: When must a firm furnish a new customer a copy of the account record, and how often after that?
notes.back: Within thirty days of opening the account, then at intervals of no more than thirty-six months.
notes.explanation: After the first copy, updates follow at least every three years.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-3 (Records to be made), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 240.17a-3(a)(17)(i)(B)”, p. 7
notes.evidence: to each customer or owner who opened an account after the effective date of this section within thirty days of the opening of the account, and thereafter at intervals no greater than thirty-six months

notes.front: What must a confirmation disclose about the trade itself?
notes.back: The date and time (or that time is available on written request), and the identity, price and number of shares or units.
notes.explanation: Rule 10b-10 lists these first among the required disclosures.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.10b-10 (Confirmation of transactions), eCFR, “§ 240.10b-10(a)(1)”
notes.evidence: The date and time of the transaction (or the fact that the time of the transaction will be furnished upon written request to such customer) and the identity, price, and number of shares or units

notes.front: What must a confirmation say about the capacity in which the broker-dealer acted?
notes.back: Whether it acted as agent (for the customer, another person or both) or as principal, and if principal, whether it is a market maker.
notes.explanation: Rule 10b-10 lists four possible roles: agent for the customer, agent for another, agent for both, or principal.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.10b-10 (Confirmation of transactions), eCFR, “§ 240.10b-10(a)(2)”
notes.evidence: Whether the broker or dealer is acting as agent for such customer, as agent for some other person, as agent for both such customer and some other person, or as principal for its own account; and if the broker or dealer is acting as principal, whether it is a market maker in the security

notes.front: Rule 2231 generally requires a general securities member to send customer account statements at least once each {{c1::calendar quarter}}.
notes.explanation: The order notes an exception for accounts carried on a delivery-versus-payment basis.
notes.source: SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rule 2231 (Customer Account Statements), 87 FR (7 June 2022), “Background”, p. 1
notes.evidence: at least once each calendar quarter, send account statements to customers containing a description of any securities positions, money balances or account activity in the accounts since the prior account statements were sent, except if carried on a Delivery Versus Payment/Receive Versus Payment basis.

notes.front: Under Rule 3150, when may a firm hold a customer’s mail?
notes.back: For a specific time period, in line with the customer’s written instructions, if the firm meets specified conditions.
notes.explanation: The rule replaced an older provision with strict time limits on holding mail.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA supervision rules, including Rule 3150 (Holding of Customer Mail), 78 FR (30 December 2013), “Summary of the proposal”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Replacing NASD Rule 3110(i) (Holding of Customer Mail) and its strict time limits for holding customer mail with proposed FINRA Rule 3150 (Holding of Customer Mail), which generally allows a member to hold a customer’s mail for a specific time period in accordance with the customer’s written instructions if the member meets specified conditions;

notes.front: When must a firm update its BCP, and how often must it review it?
notes.back: Upon any material change; and review it at least annually.
notes.explanation: The notice gives both as requirements of the rule adopted as Rule 4370.
notes.source: SEC notice of FINRA proposal to adopt Rule 4370 (Business Continuity Plans and Emergency Contact Information), 74 FR (15 June 2009), “Purpose”, p. 2
notes.evidence: further requires members to update their business continuity plans upon any material change and, at a minimum, conduct an annual review of their plans.
notes.validAsOf: 2009-06-15 · FINRA Rule 4370 as proposed in 2009; later amendments not checked

notes.front: How must a firm disclose its BCP arrangements to customers?
notes.back: In writing at account opening, by posting on its website (if any), and by mailing on request.
notes.explanation: Three channels are named as the minimum.
notes.source: SEC notice of FINRA proposal to adopt Rule 4370 (Business Continuity Plans and Emergency Contact Information), 74 FR (15 June 2009), “Purpose”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Each member must make this disclosure, at a minimum, in writing to customers at account opening, by posting it on the member’s Web site (if the member maintains a Web site), and by mailing it to customers upon request.
notes.validAsOf: 2009-06-15 · FINRA Rule 4370 as proposed in 2009; later amendments not checked

notes.front: Under the customer protection rule, what must a broker-dealer do with customers’ fully-paid and excess margin securities?
notes.back: Promptly obtain and then keep physical possession or control of them.
notes.explanation: The duty covers excess margin securities as well as fully-paid ones.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15c3-3 (Customer protection), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 240.15c3-3(b)(1)”, p. 3
notes.evidence: A broker or dealer shall promptly obtain and shall thereafter maintain the physical possession or control of all fully-paid securities and excess margin securities carried by a broker or dealer for the account of customers.

notes.front: What are two things Reg S-P does, according to its purpose section?
notes.back: Requires privacy notices to customers; and sets when nonpublic personal information may be disclosed to nonaffiliated third parties.
notes.explanation: Notice to customers comes first in the rule’s list of purposes.
notes.source: 17 CFR 248.1 (Regulation S-P purpose and scope), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 248.1(a)”, p. 1
notes.evidence: (1) Requires a financial institution to provide notice to customers about its privacy policies and practices; (2) Describes the conditions under which a financial institution may disclose nonpublic personal information

notes.front: Under Reg S-P, a firm must give a new customer its initial privacy notice not later than {{c1::when it establishes the customer relationship}}.
notes.explanation: The notice can come earlier, but no later than the start of the relationship.
notes.source: 17 CFR 248.4 (Initial privacy notice), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 248.4(a)(1)”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Customer. An individual who becomes your customer, not later than when you establish a customer relationship

notes.front: How often must a firm give customers a privacy notice after the first, and what does “annually” mean?
notes.back: Not less than annually, meaning at least once in any period of 12 consecutive months while the relationship lasts.
notes.explanation: The rule allows exceptions, set out in its paragraph (e).
notes.source: 17 CFR 248.5 (Annual privacy notice), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 248.5(a)(1)”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Except as provided by paragraph (e) of this section, you must provide a clear and conspicuous notice to customers that accurately reflects your privacy policies and practices not less than annually during the continuation of the customer relationship. Annually means at least once in any period of 12 consecutive months during which that relationship exists.

notes.front: Before disclosing NPI to a nonaffiliated third party, what must the firm give the consumer, besides notice?
notes.back: A reasonable opportunity to opt out of the disclosure; it may disclose only if the consumer does not opt out.
notes.explanation: Silence after a reasonable opportunity lets the disclosure go ahead.
notes.source: 17 CFR 248.10 (Limits on disclosure; opt out), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 248.10(a)”, p. 1
notes.evidence: You have given the consumer a reasonable opportunity, before you disclose the information to the nonaffiliated third party, to opt out of the disclosure; and (iv) The consumer does not opt out.

notes.front: What written policies does Reg S-P require to safeguard customer information, and what must they aim to do?
notes.back: Administrative, technical and physical safeguards, designed to ensure security and confidentiality and protect against threats and unauthorised access.
notes.explanation: The policies must be written, and must cover integrity as well as security.
notes.source: 17 CFR 248.30 (Regulation S-P safeguards and disposal), eCFR, “§ 248.30(a)(1)–(2)”
notes.evidence: that address administrative, technical, and physical safeguards for the protection of customer information. (2) Objectives. These written policies and procedures must be reasonably designed to: (i) Ensure the security and confidentiality of customer information; (ii) Protect against any anticipated threats or hazards to the security or integrity of customer information;

notes.front: Under Reg S-P, notice to affected individuals of unauthorised access must be given as soon as practicable, but not later than {{c1::30 days}} after becoming aware of it.
notes.explanation: Only the Attorney General can authorise a delay, on national security or public safety grounds.
notes.source: 17 CFR 248.30 (Regulation S-P safeguards and disposal), eCFR, “§ 248.30(a)(4)”
notes.evidence: must provide the notice as soon as practicable, but not later than 30 days, after becoming aware that unauthorized access to or use of customer information has occurred or is reasonably likely to have occurred unless the United States Attorney General determines that the notice required under this rule poses a substantial risk to national security or public safety
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: Does naming a trusted contact person give that person authority over the account?
notes.back: No: no authority to act for the customer, execute transactions or engage in activity in the account.
notes.explanation: It also does not make the person a power of attorney, guardian, trustee or executor.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Trusted Contact”, “Trusted Contact”
notes.evidence: Naming someone as a trusted contact does not give that person any authority to act on your behalf, execute transactions or engage in activity in your account. It also does not make that person a power of attorney, legal guardian, trustee or executor.

notes.front: A trusted contact must be at least {{c1::18}} years old.
notes.explanation: The glossary adds that more than one trusted contact may be named.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Trusted Contact”, “Trusted Contact”
notes.evidence: A trusted contact must be age 18 or older. They may be a family member, attorney, accountant or another third-party you believe would respect your privacy and know how to handle the responsibility. You may also choose to add more than one trusted contact to your account.

notes.front: What must firms do about a trusted contact person under the amended Rule 4512?
notes.back: Make reasonable efforts to obtain the name of and contact information for a trusted contact person for a customer’s account.
notes.explanation: The same change let firms place temporary holds on disbursements where exploitation is suspected.
notes.source: SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rule 4512 and new Rule 2165, 82 FR (9 February 2017), “Introduction”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Require members to make reasonable efforts to obtain the name of and contact information for a trusted contact person for a customer’s account; and (2) permit members to place temporary holds on disbursements of funds or securities from the accounts of specified customers

notes.front: Under Rule 3210, what must an associated person obtain before opening an account at another member firm?
notes.back: Prior written consent from their employer member firm; they must also notify the executing firm in writing.
notes.explanation: Written notice to the other firm is the second duty.
notes.source: SEC notice of FINRA rule change to Rule 3210 (Accounts at Other Broker-Dealers and Financial Institutions), 91 FR (7 July 2026), “Background”, p. 2
notes.evidence: The rule places obligations on associated persons when opening a specified account at another member firm (‘‘executing member’’) or other financial institution to, (1) obtain prior written consent from their employer member firm (‘‘employer member’’),11 and (2) notify in writing

notes.front: Must correspondence be filed with the self-regulator or approved by a principal before use?
notes.back: No. It is subject to the content standards, supervision, review and recordkeeping, but not filing or pre-use approval.
notes.explanation: The order says content standards still apply to correspondence.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rule 2210 (Communications with the Public), 77 FR (4 April 2012), “III.A.1”, p. 3
notes.evidence: subject to the content standards of proposed FINRA Rule 2210, but would not require it to be filed with FINRA and would not subject it to the principal pre-use approval requirement. Instead, correspondence would be subject to the supervision, review and recordkeeping requirements
notes.validAsOf: 2012-04-04 · FINRA Rule 2210 as approved in 2012; later amendments not checked

notes.front: When must certain retail communications be filed with the self-regulator?
notes.back: Depending on the communication, at least 10 business days before first use, or within 10 business days of first use.
notes.explanation: Which of the two applies depends on the type of communication.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rule 2210 (Communications with the Public), 77 FR (4 April 2012), “III.C Filing Requirements”, p. 10
notes.evidence: certain retail communications either at least 10 business days prior to first use or publication, or within 10 business days of first use or publication, depending on the communication.
notes.validAsOf: 2012-04-04 · FINRA Rule 2210 as approved in 2012; later amendments not checked

notes.front: Must a principal approve a communication before it is filed with the self-regulator?
notes.back: Yes, even if it would otherwise fall under an exception to the principal approval requirement.
notes.explanation: The notice says an appropriately qualified principal must approve any filed communication.
notes.source: SEC notice of FINRA proposal to adopt Rule 2210 (Communications with the Public), 76 FR (3 August 2011), “Approval and recordkeeping”, p. 4
notes.evidence: an appropriately qualified principal must approve any communication that is filed with the Department, even if a communication otherwise would come under an exception to the principal approval requirements
notes.validAsOf: 2012-04-04 · FINRA Rule 2210 as approved in 2012; later amendments not checked

notes.front: Without prior consent, between what hours may a telemarketer call a person’s home?
notes.back: Between 8:00 am and 9:00 pm, local time at the called person’s location.
notes.explanation: Calls outside those hours are an abusive telemarketing practice under the rule.
notes.source: 16 CFR 310.4 (Abusive telemarketing acts or practices), CFR 2026 edition, “§ 310.4(c)”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Without the prior consent of a person, it is an abusive telemarketing act or practice and a violation of this part for a telemarketer to engage in outbound telephone calls to a person’s residence at any time other than between 8:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m. local time at the called person’s location.

notes.front: Under the TSR, when is it abusive to call a person whose number is on the national do-not-call registry?
notes.back: Unless the seller can show the person’s express written agreement to receive calls, among limited exceptions.
notes.explanation: The agreement must be express and in writing.
notes.source: 16 CFR 310.4 (Abusive telemarketing acts or practices), CFR 2026 edition, “§ 310.4(b)(1)(iii)”, p. 4
notes.evidence: telephone calls to induce the purchase of goods or services unless the seller or telemarketer: (1) Can demonstrate that the seller has obtained the express agreement, in writing, of such person to place calls to that person.

notes.front: Under Rule 3230, how long must a firm honour a person’s request not to receive its calls?
notes.back: Indefinitely: the record of the request must be kept indefinitely, not for only five years.
notes.explanation: The earlier limit of five years no longer applies.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3230 (Telemarketing), 77 FR (3 February 2012), “II. Description of the Proposal”, p. 1
notes.evidence: These include a provision requiring members making outbound telephone calls to maintain a record of a person’s request not to receive such calls indefinitely rather than for only five years.
notes.validAsOf: 2012-02-03 · FINRA Rule 3230 as approved in 2012; later amendments not checked

notes.front: Who is a retail customer under Reg BI?
notes.back: A natural person, or their legal representative, who receives a recommendation and uses it primarily for personal, family or household purposes.
notes.explanation: Both limbs must be met.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15l-1 (Regulation Best Interest), eCFR, “§ 240.15l-1(b)(1)”
notes.evidence: Retail customer means a natural person, or the legal representative of such natural person, who: (i) Receives a recommendation of any securities transaction or investment strategy involving securities from a broker, dealer, or a natural person who is an associated person of a broker or dealer; and (ii) Uses the recommendation primarily for personal, family, or household purposes.

notes.front: Under Reg BI’s disclosure obligation, what must be given to the retail customer, and when?
notes.back: Full and fair written disclosure of all material facts about the relationship, prior to or at the time of the recommendation.
notes.explanation: It must be in writing and come no later than the recommendation.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15l-1 (Regulation Best Interest), eCFR, “§ 240.15l-1(a)(2)(i)”
notes.evidence: The broker, dealer, or natural person who is an associated person of a broker or dealer, prior to or at the time of the recommendation, provides the retail customer, in writing, full and fair disclosure of: (A) All material facts relating to the scope and terms of the relationship with the retail customer

notes.front: Which Reg BI obligation requires reasonable diligence, care and skill to understand a recommendation’s risks, rewards and costs?
notes.back: The care obligation.
notes.explanation: It asks for an understanding of costs as well as risks and rewards.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15l-1 (Regulation Best Interest), eCFR, “§ 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)”
notes.evidence: Care obligation. The broker, dealer, or natural person who is an associated person of a broker or dealer, in making the recommendation, exercises reasonable diligence, care, and skill to: (A) Understand the potential risks, rewards, and costs associated with the recommendation, and have a reasonable basis to believe that the recommendation could be in the best interest

notes.front: Under Reg BI’s care obligation, what must be true of a series of recommended transactions taken together?
notes.back: It must not be excessive and must be in the customer’s best interest in light of their investment profile.
notes.explanation: This applies even if each transaction is in the customer’s best interest viewed in isolation.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15l-1 (Regulation Best Interest), eCFR, “§ 240.15l-1(a)(2)(ii)(C)”
notes.evidence: Have a reasonable basis to believe that a series of recommended transactions, even if in the retail customer's best interest when viewed in isolation, is not excessive and is in the retail customer's best interest when taken together in light of the retail customer's investment profile

notes.front: Under Reg BI’s conflict of interest obligation, what must the firm’s written policies do, at a minimum, with conflicts tied to recommendations?
notes.back: Identify them and at least disclose them, or eliminate them.
notes.explanation: Disclosure is the minimum; elimination is the alternative.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15l-1 (Regulation Best Interest), eCFR, “§ 240.15l-1(a)(2)(iii)”
notes.evidence: Conflict of interest obligation. The broker or dealer establishes, maintains, and enforces written policies and procedures reasonably designed to: (A) Identify and at a minimum disclose, in accordance with paragraph (a)(2)(i) of this section, or eliminate, all conflicts of interest associated with such recommendations;

notes.front: What does Reg BI’s compliance obligation require?
notes.back: Written policies and procedures reasonably designed to achieve compliance with Reg BI as a whole.
notes.explanation: They are in addition to the conflict-of-interest policies.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15l-1 (Regulation Best Interest), eCFR, “§ 240.15l-1(a)(2)(iv)”
notes.evidence: Compliance obligation. In addition to the policies and procedures required by paragraph (a)(2)(iii) of this section, the broker or dealer establishes, maintains, and enforces written policies and procedures reasonably designed to achieve compliance with Regulation Best Interest.

notes.front: When must a broker-dealer first deliver Form CRS to a retail investor?
notes.back: Before or at the earliest of: a recommendation, placing an order, or opening a brokerage account.
notes.explanation: Whichever of the three comes first sets the deadline.
notes.evidence: Deliver to each retail investor your current Form CRS before or at the earliest of: (i) A recommendation of an account type, a securities transaction; or an investment strategy involving securities; (ii) Placing an order for the retail investor; or (iii) The opening of a brokerage account for the retail investor.

notes.front: What are two of the purposes for which Rule 2090’s “essential facts” about a customer are required?
notes.back: Any two of: servicing the account; following special handling instructions; understanding who may act for the customer; complying with laws and rules.
notes.explanation: The supplementary material defines essential facts by these four purposes.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rules 2090 (Know Your Customer) and 2111 (Suitability), 75 FR 71479 (23 November 2010), “A. Proposed FINRA Rule 2090”, p. 2
notes.evidence: ‘‘essential facts’’ as those ‘‘required to (a) Effectively service the customer’s account, (b) act in accordance with any special handling instructions for the account, (c) understand the authority of each person acting on behalf of the customer, and (d) comply with applicable laws, regulations, and rules.’’

notes.front: What are three factors in a customer’s investment profile under the suitability rule?
notes.back: Any three of: age, other investments, financial situation and needs, tax status, objectives, experience, time horizon, liquidity needs, risk tolerance.
notes.explanation: The list is open: it includes any other information the customer discloses.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rules 2090 (Know Your Customer) and 2111 (Suitability), 75 FR 71479 (23 November 2010), “B. Proposed FINRA Rule 2111”, p. 3
notes.evidence: which ‘‘includes, but is not limited to, the customer’s age, other investments, financial situation and needs, tax status, investment objectives, investment experience, investment time horizon, liquidity needs, risk tolerance, and any other information the customer may disclose
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rule 2111 as amended in 2020: applies only where Reg BI does not

notes.front: Under reasonable-basis suitability, what does recommending a security without understanding its risks and rewards amount to?
notes.back: A violation of the suitability rule.
notes.explanation: Reasonable diligence must give the firm an understanding of the product’s potential risks and rewards.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rules 2090 (Know Your Customer) and 2111 (Suitability), 75 FR 71479 (23 November 2010), “Footnote 48”, p. 5
notes.evidence: A member’s or associated person’s reasonable diligence must provide the member or associated person with an understanding of the potential risks and rewards associated with the recommended security or strategy. The lack of such an understanding when recommending a security or strategy violates the suitability rule.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rule 2111 as amended in 2020: applies only where Reg BI does not

notes.front: Does the suitability rule cover a recommendation to hold a security?
notes.back: Yes: investment strategies include an explicit recommendation to hold a security or securities.
notes.explanation: Advice to do nothing with a position can still be a recommendation.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rules 2090 (Know Your Customer) and 2111 (Suitability), 75 FR 71479 (23 November 2010), “Explicit recommendations to hold”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Amendment No. 1 would amend Supplementary Material .03 to state that investment strategies would include, among other things, an explicit recommendation to hold a security or securities.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rule 2111 as amended in 2020: applies only where Reg BI does not

notes.front: Is general financial and investment information, such as explaining diversification, covered by the suitability rule?
notes.back: No, as long as it does not include a recommendation of a particular security.
notes.explanation: The exclusion is lost if the material recommends a particular security, alone or combined with other communications.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rules 2090 (Know Your Customer) and 2111 (Suitability), 75 FR 71479 (23 November 2010), “B. Proposed FINRA Rule 2111”, p. 3
notes.evidence: the proposed supplementary material would exclude the following communications from the coverage of Rule 2111 as long as they do not include (standing alone or in combination with other communications) a recommendation of a particular security or securities: • General financial and investment information
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rule 2111 as amended in 2020: applies only where Reg BI does not

notes.front: What two conditions must both be met for the institutional-customer exemption from customer-specific suitability?
notes.back: A reasonable basis to believe the institution can evaluate risks independently; and the institution affirmatively indicates it is exercising independent judgement.
notes.explanation: The order stresses that the exemption applies only if both parts are met.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rules 2090 (Know Your Customer) and 2111 (Suitability), 75 FR 71479 (23 November 2010), “Footnote 25”, p. 3
notes.evidence: the institutional-customer exemption applies only if both parts of the two-part test are met: (1) There is a reasonable basis to believe that the institutional customer is capable of evaluating investment risks independently, in general and with regard to particular transactions and investment strategies, and (2) the institutional customer affirmatively indicates that it is exercising independent judgment in evaluating recommendations.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rule 2111 as amended in 2020: applies only where Reg BI does not

notes.front: In her cash account Priya buys 200 shares on Tuesday and, before paying, sells them on Wednesday at a profit. What may follow?
notes.back: B: buying and selling before paying is freeriding, which may require a 90-day freeze.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, since she made a profit
B) Her broker may have to freeze the cash account for 90 days
C) The trade is converted into a margin loan
D) A Currency Transaction Report must be filed
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: profit does not matter. C is wrong: a cash account does not borrow. D is wrong: no currency transaction over $10,000 is described.
notes.explanation: Freeriding is not permitted under Reg T.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Cash Account”, “Cash Account”
notes.evidence: If an investor buys and sells a security before paying for it, the investor is “freeriding” which is not permitted under Regulation T and may require the investor’s broker to “freeze” the investor’s cash account for 90 days.

notes.front: Tom wants to buy $30,000 of a listed stock (a margin equity security) in his margin account, and no higher exchange percentage applies. What is the minimum Reg T margin he must provide?
notes.back: B: $15,000, which is 50 percent of the $30,000 market value.
notes.choicesExplained: A is 25 percent, the maintenance figure. C is full payment, as in a cash account. D is only the minimum margin deposit.
notes.explanation: Reg T sets 50 percent of current market value for margin equity securities.
notes.source: 12 CFR 220.12 (Regulation T), eCFR, “§ 220.12(a)”
notes.evidence: 50 percent of the current market value of the security or the percentage set by the regulatory authority where the trade occurs, whichever is greater.

notes.front: Ana buys $20,000 of stock, borrowing $10,000. The stock falls to $14,000. Her firm uses a 35 percent maintenance requirement. Is she below it?
notes.choices:
A) No: her equity of $4,000 exceeds 25 percent of $14,000
B) Yes: any fall in price triggers a margin call
C) No: equity is measured against the original $20,000
D) Yes: her $4,000 equity is below the $4,900 the firm requires
notes.choicesExplained: A applies the 25 percent minimum, but the firm’s higher house figure governs. C is wrong: the requirement is on current market value. B is wrong: only falling below the requirement matters.
notes.explanation: Equity is the securities’ value less the amount owed, compared with the firm’s requirement.
notes.source: SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy, Investor Bulletin: Understanding Margin Accounts, “Maintenance requirements”
notes.evidence: The equity in your margin account is the value of your securities less how much you owe to your brokerage firm. FINRA rules require this “maintenance requirement” to be at least 25 percent of the total market value of the margin securities.

notes.front: A new customer phones to buy listed call options. The firm has not yet sent her the options disclosure document. What should it do?
notes.back: D: no options order may be accepted until the options disclosure document has been furnished.
notes.choices:
A) Take the order and post the document afterwards
B) Take the order in a cash account instead
C) Take the order if she is an accredited investor
D) Not accept the order until it has furnished the document
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the document must come first. C and B are wrong: the rule has no such exceptions for this customer.
notes.explanation: Rule 9b-1 bars accepting the order and approving the account alike.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.9b-1 (Options disclosure document), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 240.9b-1(d)(1)”, p. 2
notes.evidence: No broker or dealer shall accept an order from a customer to purchase or sell an option contract relating to an options class that is the subject of a definitive options disclosure document, or approve the customer’s account for the trading of such option, unless the broker or dealer furnishes or has furnished

notes.front: A representative with discretion over a retired teacher’s modest account trades it forty times a month. Which rule problem is most direct?
notes.back: B: excessive trading in a discretionary account is a defined fraudulent device.
notes.choices:
A) None, since he has written discretion
B) Transactions excessive in size or frequency for the account’s resources and character
C) A missing privacy notice
D) Structuring
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: discretion does not permit excessive trading. C and D are unrelated to trading frequency.
notes.explanation: Rule 15c1-7 measures excess against the account’s financial resources and character.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15c1-7 (Discretionary accounts), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 240.15c1-7(a)”, p. 1
notes.evidence: any transactions or purchase or sale which are excessive in size or frequency in view of the financial resources and character of such account.

notes.front: Leo pays his firm 1.2 percent a year of his account’s value, and that single fee covers management, trading and administration. What kind of account is this?
notes.back: A: a wrap account, where one fee based on account value covers all those expenses.
notes.choices:
A) A wrap account
B) A commission-based account
C) A discretionary account
D) A cash account
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: commissions are charged per transaction as agent. C and D describe authority and payment, not how fees are charged.
notes.explanation: The fee is based on market value and covers management, brokerage and administrative expenses.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Wrap Account”, “Wrap Account”
notes.evidence: A wrap account is an investment account where a "wrapped" fee or fees cover all of the management, brokerage and administrative expenses for the account. The fee or fees are generally based on the total market value of the investment account.

notes.front: Maya and her brother hold property as joint tenants with right of survivorship. Maya dies. Who holds the property?
notes.back: B: the surviving joint tenant.
notes.choices:
A) Maya’s estate, for her half
B) Her brother, as surviving tenant
C) The two are split by a court
D) The broker, until probate
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D ignore survivorship: the survivor’s basis takes in the part included in Maya’s estate.
notes.explanation: With right of survivorship, the dead owner’s share passes to the surviving joint tenant; Publication 559 treats the survivor as acquiring it.
notes.source: IRS Publication 559, Survivors, Executors, and Administrators, ““Joint interest””, p. 20
notes.evidence: Figure the surviving tenant's new basis of jointly owned property (joint tenancy or tenancy by the entirety) by adding the surviving tenant's original basis in the property to the value of the part of the property included in the decedent's estate

notes.front: Grace puts investments into a written living trust for her children and keeps full control during her lifetime. Which kind of trust is this?
notes.back: C: a formal revocable (living) trust.
notes.choices:
A) UTMA custodial account
B) Irrevocable trust
C) Revocable trust
D) Joint account
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: she has not given up the power to change it. A is for a minor, via a custodian. D has co-owners, not beneficiaries.
notes.explanation: Formal revocable trusts are known as living or family trusts, with the owner in control during life.
notes.source: FDIC, Your Insured Deposits, “Trust Accounts”
notes.evidence: Formal Revocable Trusts - known as living or family trusts – are written trusts created for estate planning purposes. The owner controls the deposits and other assets in the trust during his or her lifetime.

notes.front: Shares were given to Sam under UTMA when he was six. He has now reached his state’s age of majority. What happens?
notes.back: D: the minor automatically receives control on reaching the age of majority.
notes.choices:
A) The custodian keeps control until Sam is 30
B) The shares pass to a trust
C) The shares return to the donor
D) Sam automatically receives control of the assets
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: custody ends at the state age of majority. C is wrong: the transfer was irrevocable. B is wrong: no trust is involved.
notes.explanation: Control shifts from custodian to the young person without any further act.
notes.source: Social Security POMS SI 01120.205, Uniform Transfers to Minors Act, “C. UTMA provisions”
notes.evidence: the minor automatically receives control of the assets upon attainment of the age of majority established by State law.

notes.front: Ruth is 52 and earns $40,000 in 2026. What is the most she can put into her traditional and Roth IRAs combined for 2026?
notes.back: B: $8,600, the 2026 limit for someone aged 50 or older.
notes.choicesExplained: A and D are the 2024–2025 figures. C is the 2026 limit for under-50s.
notes.explanation: Her compensation exceeds the limit, so the dollar limit applies.
notes.source: IRS, Retirement topics: IRA contribution limits, “Contribution limits”
notes.evidence: For 2026, the total contributions you make each year to all of your traditional IRAs and Roth IRAs can’t be more than: $7,500 ($8,600 if you’re age 50 or older), or If less, your taxable compensation for the year
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: An employer promises workers a pension of a set amount each month at retirement and takes the investment risk. Which plan type is this?
notes.back: C: a defined benefit plan.
notes.choices:
A) 401(k) plan
B) Defined contribution plan
C) Defined benefit plan
D) Roth IRA
notes.choicesExplained: B and A promise no specific payment and leave the risk with the employee. D is an individual account.
notes.explanation: A promised monthly benefit with the employer bearing the risk marks a defined benefit plan.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Defined Benefit Plan”, “Defined Benefit Plan”
notes.evidence: Employers sponsor defined benefit plans and promise the plan's investments will provide you with a specified monthly benefit at retirement. The employer bears the investment risks.

notes.front: Carlos, a traditional IRA owner, turns 73 in 2026. What is the latest he can take his first RMD, and when is the second due?
notes.back: D: first by 1 April 2027, second by 31 December 2027.
notes.choices:
A) 31 December 2026; 31 December 2027
B) 1 April 2028; 31 December 2028
C) 1 April 2026; 31 December 2026
D) 1 April 2027; 31 December 2027
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the permitted delay. C is too early. B is a year too late.
notes.explanation: The first RMD may be delayed until 1 April of the year after he reaches 73.
notes.source: IRS, Retirement plan and IRA required minimum distributions FAQs, “Q3”
notes.evidence: You must take your first required minimum distribution for the year in which you reach age 73. However, you can delay taking the first RMD until April 1 of the following year.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: After depositing crime proceeds in a bank, a gang wires the money through a dozen accounts in different names to confuse anyone tracing it. Which step is the wiring?
notes.back: C: layering, moving money around to create confusion.
notes.choices:
A) Placement
B) Integration
C) Layering
D) Structuring
notes.choicesExplained: A is the first entry into the system (the deposit). B is the final step, when the money appears clean. D is splitting cash to evade reports.
notes.explanation: FinCEN describes layering as moving the money, sometimes through numerous accounts.
notes.source: FinCEN, History of Anti-Money Laundering Laws, “History of Anti-Money Laundering Laws”
notes.evidence: Then, the money is moved around to create confusion, sometimes by wiring or transferring through numerous accounts.

notes.front: A customer with $28,000 in cash deposits $9,300 on each of three days, saying he wants to “avoid paperwork”. What is this?
notes.back: D: structuring, splitting a sum over $10,000 to evade reporting.
notes.choices:
A) Free-riding
B) Layering
C) Normal cash management
D) Structuring
notes.choicesExplained: B is moving funds through accounts. C ignores his stated purpose. A is a cash-account payment violation.
notes.explanation: No single deposit needs to exceed $10,000 for it to be structuring.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1010.100 (General definitions), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 1010.100(xx)”, p. 8
notes.evidence: the breaking down of a single sum of currency exceeding $10,000 into smaller sums, including sums at or below $10,000

notes.front: A firm cannot form a reasonable belief that it knows a new applicant’s true identity. What must its CIP already address?
notes.back: A: the CIP must describe responses, including when not to open an account.
notes.choices:
A) When it should not open the account, among other responses
B) Nothing, since verification is optional
C) Filing a CTR
D) Asking the applicant’s trusted contact to verify
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: verification procedures are required. C concerns cash transactions. D misuses the trusted contact.
notes.explanation: Refusing to open the account is one of the responses the procedures describe.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.220 (Customer identification programs for broker-dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.220(a)(2)(iii)”
notes.evidence: The CIP must include procedures for responding to circumstances in which the broker-dealer cannot form a reasonable belief that it knows the true identity of a customer. These procedures should describe: (A) When the broker-dealer should not open an account;

notes.front: A client asks his representative whether the firm has “reported him” after a string of odd wires. The firm has filed a SAR. What may she say?
notes.back: B: she may not disclose the SAR or anything revealing it exists.
notes.choices:
A) Confirm it, to be honest with him
B) Nothing that would reveal the SAR’s existence
C) Confirm it only if he promises confidentiality
D) Show him the SAR
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D all disclose the SAR, which the rule forbids.
notes.explanation: The SAR and information revealing it are confidential.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.320 (Suspicious activity reports by brokers or dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.320(e)”
notes.evidence: A SAR, and any information that would reveal the existence of a SAR, are confidential and shall not be disclosed except as authorized in this paragraph (e).

notes.front: On 1 March a firm detects a suspicious $40,000 transfer but cannot yet identify a suspect. What is the latest it may file the SAR?
notes.back: D: up to 60 calendar days after initial detection when no suspect is identified.
notes.choices:
A) 31 March
B) No SAR is needed without a suspect
C) 1 June
D) 30 April (60 days after detection)
notes.choicesExplained: A is the normal 30-day limit. C exceeds 60 days. B is wrong: the amount exceeds $5,000.
notes.explanation: The extra 30 days exist only to identify a suspect.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.320 (Suspicious activity reports by brokers or dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.320(b)(3)”
notes.evidence: If no suspect is identified on the date of such initial detection, a broker-dealer may delay filing a SAR for an additional 30 calendar days to identify a suspect, but in no case shall reporting be delayed more than 60 calendar days after the date of such initial detection.

notes.front: A customer deposits exactly $10,000 in currency, in one transaction, with nothing suspicious about it. Is a CTR required?
notes.back: A: a CTR is required for currency transactions of more than $10,000.
notes.choices:
A) No: the threshold is more than $10,000
B) Yes, at $10,000 or more
C) Only if a SAR is also filed
D) Only for withdrawals
notes.choicesExplained: B misstates the threshold. C confuses the two reports. D is wrong: deposits are covered.
notes.explanation: The rule covers deposits, withdrawals, exchanges and transfers alike.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1010.311 (Currency transaction reports), eCFR, “§ 1010.311”
notes.evidence: shall file a report of each deposit, withdrawal, exchange of currency or other payment or transfer, by, through, or to such financial institution which involves a transaction in currency of more than $10,000

notes.front: A firm hires an outside auditor each calendar year to check whether its AML programme works. Which minimum element does this meet?
notes.back: B: annual independent testing, by firm personnel or a qualified outside party.
notes.choices:
A) Ongoing training
B) Independent testing
C) Designating an AML compliance person
D) Customer identification
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D are other elements that an audit does not satisfy.
notes.explanation: The testing must be annual, on a calendar-year basis.
notes.source: SEC notice of FINRA rule change to Rule 3310 (AML compliance program), 83 FR (8 May 2018), “Purpose”, p. 2
notes.evidence: (3) provide for annual (on a calendar-year basis) independent testing for compliance to be conducted by member firm personnel

notes.front: A firm finds that a customer is on the SDN list and blocks the account’s assets on 2 June. By when must it report the blocked property?
notes.back: A: within 10 business days from the date the property becomes blocked.
notes.choices:
A) Within 10 business days of 2 June
B) Within 30 calendar days, like a SAR
C) Only at year-end
D) Never; blocking is enough
notes.choicesExplained: B borrows the SAR deadline. C and D ignore the reporting duty.
notes.explanation: The deadline counts business days, not calendar days.
notes.source: 31 CFR 501.603 (Reports of blocked property), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 501.603(b)(1)”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Reports shall be filed within 10 business days from the date that property becomes blocked.

notes.front: Which record is kept for at least six years rather than three: an order memorandum, the blotter, or a customer complaint record?
notes.back: B: the blotter (a Rule 17a-3(a)(1) record) is kept six years; the other two, three.
notes.choices:
A) The order memorandum
B) The blotter
C) The complaint record
D) All three are kept six years
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are Rule 17a-3(a)(6) and (18) records, which Rule 17a-4 keeps for three years (FINRA Rule 4513 asks four for complaint records). D is wrong for the same reason.
notes.explanation: In both cases the first two years must be easily accessible.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-4 (Records to be preserved), eCFR, “§ 240.17a-4(a)–(b)”
notes.evidence: must preserve for a period of not less than 6 years, the first two years in an easily accessible place, all records required to be made pursuant to § 240.17a-3(a)(1) through (3)

notes.front: A firm sells a customer shares from its own inventory in a stock in which it makes a market. What must the confirmation state about capacity?
notes.back: D: principal capacity, and whether it is a market maker.
notes.choices:
A) Only the commission charged
B) That it acted as agent
C) Nothing about capacity
D) That it acted as principal and is a market maker in the stock
notes.choicesExplained: B misstates its role. C and A omit the required capacity disclosure.
notes.explanation: A principal must also disclose whether it is a market maker.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.10b-10 (Confirmation of transactions), eCFR, “§ 240.10b-10(a)(2)”
notes.evidence: or as principal for its own account; and if the broker or dealer is acting as principal, whether it is a market maker in the security

notes.front: Eve holds shares and cash at a general securities firm but makes no trades for six months. Must she still receive account statements?
notes.back: D: statements describing positions and balances go out at least quarterly.
notes.choices:
A) Only if she asks the firm to hold her mail
B) No, only after trades
C) Only once a year
D) Yes, at least once each calendar quarter
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: statements cover positions and balances, not only activity. C is too infrequent. A is unrelated.
notes.explanation: Statements describe positions, money balances or activity.
notes.source: SEC order approving amendments to FINRA Rule 2231 (Customer Account Statements), 87 FR (7 June 2022), “Background”, p. 1
notes.evidence: at least once each calendar quarter, send account statements to customers containing a description of any securities positions, money balances or account activity

notes.front: A firm moves its trading operations to a new city in June. Its BCP was last reviewed in January. What must it do?
notes.back: D: update the plan upon any material change.
notes.choices:
A) File a SAR
B) Wait for next January’s review
C) Nothing, since the plan was reviewed this year
D) Update the plan for the material change
notes.choicesExplained: B and C ignore the material-change duty. A is unrelated.
notes.explanation: Annual review is a minimum, not a substitute for updating after a material change.
notes.source: SEC notice of FINRA proposal to adopt Rule 4370 (Business Continuity Plans and Emergency Contact Information), 74 FR (15 June 2009), “Purpose”, p. 2
notes.evidence: further requires members to update their business continuity plans upon any material change and, at a minimum, conduct an annual review of their plans.
notes.validAsOf: 2009-06-15 · FINRA Rule 4370 as proposed in 2009; later amendments not checked

notes.front: A customer has fully paid for 500 shares held by her broker-dealer. What must the firm do with them?
notes.back: C: obtain and keep physical possession or control of fully-paid customer securities.
notes.choices:
A) Pledge them for its own loans
B) Lend them out freely
C) Keep physical possession or control of them
D) Return them to the issuer
notes.choicesExplained: B and A would use customer securities for the firm’s own purposes. D is not a custody duty.
notes.explanation: The rule applies to fully-paid and excess margin securities alike.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15c3-3 (Customer protection), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 240.15c3-3(b)(1)”, p. 3
notes.evidence: A broker or dealer shall promptly obtain and shall thereafter maintain the physical possession or control of all fully-paid securities and excess margin securities carried by a broker or dealer for the account of customers.

notes.front: A firm wants to sell a list of its customers’ account balances to an unaffiliated marketing company. Under Reg S-P, what must happen first?
notes.back: A: notice plus a reasonable chance to opt out, with no opt-out received.
notes.choices:
A) Notice and a reasonable opportunity to opt out, and the customer does not opt out
B) Nothing, since the firm owns its records
C) A SAR filing
D) The customers’ trusted contacts must consent
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: this is NPI going to a nonaffiliated third party. C and D are unrelated.
notes.explanation: Without a reasonable chance to opt out, the disclosure cannot be made.
notes.source: 17 CFR 248.10 (Limits on disclosure; opt out), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 248.10(a)”, p. 1
notes.evidence: You have given the consumer a reasonable opportunity, before you disclose the information to the nonaffiliated third party, to opt out of the disclosure; and (iv) The consumer does not opt out.

notes.front: On 3 May a firm becomes aware that sensitive customer information was probably accessed without authorisation. No national-security delay applies. What is the latest it may notify affected individuals?
notes.back: C: as soon as practicable, and not later than 30 days after becoming aware.
notes.choices:
A) Whenever its annual privacy notice goes out
B) 3 August
C) 2 June (30 days)
D) There is no deadline
notes.choicesExplained: B, A and D all exceed the 30-day limit.
notes.explanation: Likely unauthorised access counts, not only confirmed access.
notes.source: 17 CFR 248.30 (Regulation S-P safeguards and disposal), eCFR, “§ 248.30(a)(4)”
notes.evidence: but not later than 30 days, after becoming aware that unauthorized access to or use of customer information has occurred or is reasonably likely to have occurred
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · rules in force

notes.front: A customer’s named trusted contact person calls and asks the firm to sell the customer’s shares. What should the firm do?
notes.back: B: naming a trusted contact gives no authority to transact.
notes.choices:
A) Sell, since the customer named her
B) Refuse: a trusted contact has no authority to execute transactions
C) Sell if the order is under $10,000
D) Transfer the account to her
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D all treat the trusted contact as having authority she lacks.
notes.explanation: The trusted contact is someone to contact, not an agent.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Trusted Contact”, “Trusted Contact”
notes.evidence: Naming someone as a trusted contact does not give that person any authority to act on your behalf, execute transactions or engage in activity in your account.

notes.front: A registered representative wants to open a brokerage account at a different member firm. What must she do first?
notes.back: D: obtain prior written consent from her employer firm, and notify the other firm in writing.
notes.choices:
A) Tell her employer within a year
B) Nothing, if the account is small
C) Ask the other firm to keep it confidential
D) Get her employer firm’s prior written consent
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and A ignore the prior-consent requirement.
notes.explanation: Consent must come before the account is opened, and in writing.
notes.source: SEC notice of FINRA rule change to Rule 3210 (Accounts at Other Broker-Dealers and Financial Institutions), 91 FR (7 July 2026), “Background”, p. 2
notes.evidence: obtain prior written consent from their employer member firm (‘‘employer member’’),11 and (2) notify in writing

notes.front: A representative emails the same market commentary to 30 retail investors over two weeks. Which category is it?
notes.back: D: a retail communication, as it reached more than 25 retail investors within 30 days.
notes.choices:
A) Correspondence
B) Not a communication at all
C) Institutional communication
D) Retail communication
notes.choicesExplained: A applies to 25 or fewer. C needs institutional investors only. B is wrong: written email counts.
notes.explanation: The 25-investor, 30-day test sorts correspondence from retail communications.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rule 2210 (Communications with the Public), 77 FR (4 April 2012), “III.A.1 Retail Communication and Correspondence”, p. 3
notes.evidence: FINRA proposed to define ‘‘retail communication’’ as ‘‘any written (including electronic) communication that is distributed or made available to more than 25 retail investors within any 30 calendar-day period’’
notes.validAsOf: 2012-04-04 · FINRA Rule 2210 as approved in 2012; later amendments not checked

notes.front: A cold-caller in New York rings a prospect at home in California at 11:30 pm New York time, without consent. Is the time permitted?
notes.back: C: the 8:00 am to 9:00 pm window is measured at the called person’s location.
notes.choices:
A) No: all cold calls are banned
B) No: calls after 9:00 pm caller’s time are banned
C) Yes: it is 8:30 pm at the prospect’s location
D) Yes: calling hours apply only to charities
notes.choicesExplained: B uses the wrong time zone. A and D misstate the rule.
notes.explanation: Local time at the called person’s location decides.
notes.source: 16 CFR 310.4 (Abusive telemarketing acts or practices), CFR 2026 edition, “§ 310.4(c)”, p. 5
notes.evidence: at any time other than between 8:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m. local time at the called person’s location.

notes.front: Seven years ago a prospect asked a firm not to call him again. A new salesperson wants to call him now. May she?
notes.back: C: the firm must keep the request indefinitely.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if she calls before 9:00 pm
B) Yes: requests lapse after five years
C) No: the firm-specific request is kept indefinitely
D) Yes, if he is not on the national registry
notes.choicesExplained: B states the old five-year rule. A and D ignore the firm-specific request.
notes.explanation: The five-year limit was replaced by an indefinite one.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rule 3230 (Telemarketing), 77 FR (3 February 2012), “II. Description of the Proposal”, p. 1
notes.evidence: to maintain a record of a person’s request not to receive such calls indefinitely rather than for only five years.
notes.validAsOf: 2012-02-03 · FINRA Rule 3230 as approved in 2012; later amendments not checked

notes.front: A firm adopts written procedures to identify sales contests that reward representatives for selling one fund, and to eliminate them. Which Reg BI obligation is this?
notes.back: C: the conflict of interest obligation.
notes.choices:
A) Care obligation
B) Disclosure obligation
C) Conflict of interest obligation
D) Compliance obligation
notes.choicesExplained: B is about written disclosure to customers. A is about diligence in each recommendation. D covers Reg BI compliance generally.
notes.explanation: That obligation requires written policies to identify and disclose or eliminate conflicts.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15l-1 (Regulation Best Interest), eCFR, “§ 240.15l-1(a)(2)(iii)”
notes.evidence: Conflict of interest obligation. The broker or dealer establishes, maintains, and enforces written policies and procedures reasonably designed to: (A) Identify and at a minimum disclose, in accordance with paragraph (a)(2)(i) of this section, or eliminate, all conflicts of interest

notes.front: An existing brokerage customer opens a new account of a different type from her current one. Must the firm give her Form CRS again?
notes.back: D: deliver the current Form CRS before or at the opening of a new, different account.
notes.choices:
A) Only once a year
B) No, she already has one
C) Only if she asks within 30 days
D) Yes, before or at the time it opens the new account
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and A ignore the delivery trigger for existing customers.
notes.explanation: Opening a different type of account is one of the triggers for existing customers.
notes.evidence: Deliver to each retail investor who is an existing customer your current Form CRS before or at the time you: (i) Open a new account that is different from the retail investor's existing account(s);

notes.front: A representative recommends a complex note that suits some investors to a small charity whose account needs ready cash and cannot bear losses. Which suitability obligation is breached?
notes.back: B: customer-specific, as it is unsuitable for this particular investor.
notes.choices:
A) Reasonable-basis suitability
B) Customer-specific suitability
C) Quantitative suitability
D) Know your customer only
notes.choicesExplained: A is met if it suits some investors. C concerns the number of trades. D is about knowing facts, which the representative seems to know.
notes.explanation: A charity is not a natural person, so Reg BI does not apply and Rule 2111 does; customer-specific suitability asks about the particular investor at issue.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rules 2090 (Know Your Customer) and 2111 (Suitability), 75 FR 71479 (23 November 2010), “B. Proposed FINRA Rule 2111”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Customer specific (members must have reasonable grounds to believe a recommendation is suitable for the particular investor at issue)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rule 2111 as amended in 2020: applies only where Reg BI does not

notes.front: Each recommendation a representative makes for a small family company’s account suits it on its own, but he recommends 60 trades there in three months. Which suitability obligation is in question?
notes.back: C: quantitative suitability, about whether the number of transactions is excessive.
notes.choices:
A) Know your customer
B) Reasonable-basis suitability
C) Quantitative suitability
D) Reg S-P
notes.choicesExplained: B concerns the product in general. A concerns knowing the customer. D concerns privacy.
notes.explanation: Quantitative suitability looks at the number of recommended transactions within a period. The account belongs to a company, not a natural person, so Rule 2111 applies rather than Reg BI.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rules 2090 (Know Your Customer) and 2111 (Suitability), 75 FR 71479 (23 November 2010), “B. Proposed FINRA Rule 2111”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Quantitative (members must have a reasonable basis to believe the number of transactions recommended to a customer within a certain period is not excessive)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Rule 2111 as amended in 2020: applies only where Reg BI does not

notes.front: A new customer tells her representative her net worth is $900,000, of which $600,000 is her home. What net worth figure belongs in the account record?
notes.back: B: $300,000, since net worth in the account record excludes the value of the primary residence.
notes.choices:
A) $900,000, including the home
B) $300,000, excluding the primary residence
C) $600,000, the home alone
D) None; net worth is not recorded
notes.choicesExplained: A includes the home, which the rule excludes. C records only the home. D is wrong: net worth is a required item.
notes.explanation: Net worth sits in the rule’s list of required account-record items beside annual income and investment objectives.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.17a-3 (Records to be made), CFR 2025 edition, “§ 240.17a-3(a)(17)(i)(A)”, p. 7
notes.evidence: annual income, net worth (excluding value of primary residence), and the account’s investment objectives.

notes.front: A customer leaving for four months abroad asks her firm to hold her mail until she returns. On what basis may the firm do so under Rule 3150?
notes.back: B: for a specific time period, under her written instructions, if specified conditions are met.
notes.choices:
A) Indefinitely, on a verbal request
B) Under her written instructions, for that specific period, if the firm meets the rule’s conditions
C) Never; mail must always be sent
D) Only if her trusted contact agrees
notes.choicesExplained: A lacks the written instructions and a set period. C is wrong: holding is allowed. D invents a condition.
notes.explanation: The rule ties the hold to the customer’s own written instructions.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA supervision rules, including Rule 3150 (Holding of Customer Mail), 78 FR (30 December 2013), “Summary of the proposal”, p. 3
notes.evidence: which generally allows a member to hold a customer’s mail for a specific time period in accordance with the customer’s written instructions if the member meets specified conditions;

notes.front: What is the key difference between a cash account and a margin account?
notes.back: In a cash account you pay in full and cannot borrow; in a margin account the broker-dealer lends you cash against the account as collateral.
notes.explanation: The difference is who supplies the money: the investor alone, or partly the broker-dealer.
notes.source: SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy, Investor Bulletin: Understanding Margin Accounts, “Cash and margin accounts”
notes.evidence: A “ cash account ” is a type of brokerage account in which you must pay the full amount for securities purchased. In a cash account you cannot borrow funds from your broker-dealer to pay for transactions in the account. A “margin account” is a type of brokerage account in which your broker-dealer lends you cash

notes.front: How does a revocable trust differ from an irrevocable trust in the owner’s control?
notes.back: A revocable trust’s owner keeps control during life; an irrevocable trust’s owner gives up all power to cancel or change it.
notes.explanation: Giving up the power to cancel or change is what makes a trust irrevocable.
notes.source: FDIC, Your Insured Deposits, “Trust Accounts”
notes.evidence: Irrevocable Trusts are deposit accounts held in connection with a trust established by statute or a written trust agreement in which the owner contributes deposits or other property to the trust and gives up all power to cancel or change the trust.

notes.front: Which tax feature of a traditional IRA does a Roth IRA lack, and what does it offer instead?
notes.back: Deductible contributions: Roth contributions cannot be deducted, but qualified distributions are tax-free.
notes.explanation: The Roth moves the tax benefit from the contribution to the withdrawal.
notes.source: IRS, Roth IRAs, “Roth IRAs”
notes.evidence: You cannot deduct contributions to a Roth IRA. - If you satisfy the requirements, qualified distributions are tax-free.

notes.front: Who bears the investment risk in a defined benefit plan compared with a defined contribution plan?
notes.back: The employer in a defined benefit plan; the employee in a defined contribution plan.
notes.explanation: A defined contribution plan promises no specific payment, so the result depends on the account.
notes.source: Investor.gov glossary, “Defined Contribution Plan”, “Defined Contribution Plan”
notes.evidence: A retirement savings plan, such as a 401(k) plan, that does not promise a specific payment upon retirement. In these plans, the employee or the employer (or both) contribute to the employee's individual account. The employee bears the investment risks.

notes.front: How does the trigger for a broker-dealer’s SAR differ from that for a CTR?
notes.back: A SAR: a suspicious transaction of at least $5,000. A CTR: any currency transaction over $10,000, suspicious or not.
notes.explanation: The SAR test also needs the firm to know, suspect or have reason to suspect the transaction.
notes.source: 31 CFR 1023.320 (Suspicious activity reports by brokers or dealers), eCFR, “§ 1023.320(a)(2)”
notes.evidence: it involves or aggregates funds or other assets of at least $5,000, and the broker-dealer knows, suspects, or has reason to suspect that the transaction

notes.front: How many component obligations do the suitability rule and Reg BI each have, and what are Reg BI’s?
notes.back: Suitability has three (reasonable-basis, customer-specific, quantitative). Reg BI has four: disclosure, care, conflict of interest, compliance.
notes.explanation: Since 2020 Rule 2111 does not apply to recommendations covered by Reg BI, so for retail customers Reg BI’s four obligations govern.
notes.source: 17 CFR 240.15l-1 (Regulation Best Interest), eCFR, “§ 240.15l-1(a)(2)”
notes.evidence: Compliance obligation. In addition to the policies and procedures required by paragraph (a)(2)(iii) of this section, the broker or dealer establishes, maintains, and enforces written policies and procedures reasonably designed to achieve compliance with Regulation Best Interest.

notes.front: What single test separates correspondence from a retail communication?
notes.back: How many retail investors it reaches within any 30-calendar-day period: 25 or fewer is correspondence; more than 25 is retail.
notes.explanation: Both must be written, including electronic, communications.
notes.source: SEC order approving FINRA Rule 2210 (Communications with the Public), 77 FR (4 April 2012), “III.A.1 Retail Communication and Correspondence”, p. 3
notes.evidence: distributed or made available to more than 25 retail investors within any 30 calendar-day period’’ and ‘‘correspondence’’ as ‘‘any written (including electronic) communication that is distributed or made available to 25 or fewer retail investors within any 30 calendar-day period.’’
notes.validAsOf: 2012-04-04 · FINRA Rule 2210 as approved in 2012; later amendments not checked
